data.title: AlgoBrain BCI
data.summary: A custom bio-amplifier and embedded signal-processing prototype for device control.
data.paperTitle: A custom bio-signal interface: analog conditioning, causal processing, and event control

projects.body:
## Abstract
AlgoBrain investigates an end-to-end bio-signal interface: a custom TL074 analog front end, Arduino acquisition, stateful digital filtering, desktop signal inspection, and an envelope-triggered infrared control path. Its contribution is the integration of an observable sensing and processing chain, from electrode input to waveform, spectrum, recording, and relay state. The supplied archive contains distinct firmware variants for serial acquisition and physical control. This paper specifies their interfaces, derives the filtering and decision operations, and distinguishes intended sampling settings from the scheduling implemented in each sketch. Forehead acquisition can contain EEG, EMG, motion, and electrode artifacts; the demonstrated threshold detects signal amplitude events rather than classifying thoughts.

**Keywords:** bio-amplifier; EEG/EMG; embedded acquisition; causal filtering; spectral inspection; envelope control.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/projects/algobrain-abstract-v2.webp" width={1672} height={941} alt="Conceptual sensing, filtering, observation and control workbench" caption="Concept illustration of the sensing-to-control workflow. The hardware, electrode arrangement, and waveforms are illustrative; the source-derived scientific figures below specify the actual implementation." />

<ProjectAlbum />

## System specification
### 2.1 Analog acquisition and digital observability
The project combines a custom PCB and enclosure with an Arduino-based acquisition board. The project notes describe a forehead channel with ear-mounted references and a four-stage TL074 signal path: differential acquisition, high-pass filtering, gain, and low-pass filtering. The original enclosure photograph in the gallery shows the amplifier board, passive components, wiring, and Arduino module together.

The analog front end conditions a small differential input before digitization. High-pass behavior reduces slow baseline drift; gain brings a changing signal into a useful acquisition range; low-pass behavior limits faster components. These are functional roles from the project documentation. Calibrated gain, bandwidth, input-referred noise, and common-mode rejection were not established by the supplied recordings and code alone.

| Subsystem | Reviewed artifact | Observable output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Analog front end | Circuit/PCB archive and original prototype | Conditioned voltage at Arduino A0 |
| Serial acquisition | `simple_data_sender.ino` | Raw ADC value, filtered value, cycle counter |
| Desktop inspection | `algobrain_visualizer.py` | Raw/filtered plots, spectrum, statistics, CSV |
| Event controller | IR LED firmware variant | Envelope threshold, LED state, NEC transmissions |
| Physical receiver | `final_reciver_AlgoBrain.ino` | Relay state and red/green indicators |

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/algobrain/research/algobrain-hardware-styled.webp" width={1659} height={948} alt="AlgoBrain forehead electrodes, four-stage TL074 front end, custom PCB and Arduino acquisition" caption="Figure 1. Functional hardware architecture, grounded in the project notes and original prototype photograph. Waveform illustrations are schematic; no calibrated circuit gain or cutoff values are implied." />

### 2.2 Two firmware contracts
The serial sender targets $f_s=500$ Hz at 115200 baud. It reads A0, applies four second-order filter sections, and writes three comma-separated fields: raw integer, filtered value to four decimal places, and cycle counter. The counter wraps after 1000 samples and emits a `CYCLE_RESET` marker. The desktop reader accepts three-field numeric lines; the marker does not become a sample.

The archived IR controller instead writes signal/envelope pairs and adds amplitude-based actuation. These are separate protocols. The three-field desktop reader should not be described as directly consuming the controller's two-field stream without an adapter.

## Method
### 3.1 Differential input and mixed biological sources
Let the electrode input difference be

$$
v_d(t)=v_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-v_{\mathrm{ref}}(t).
\tag{1}
$$

The measured signal includes the intended physiological component together with muscle activity, movement, electrode contact effects, and electrical interference. Differential conditioning and filtering improve inspectability, but a large filtered amplitude does not identify the source of that amplitude. Forehead demonstrations must therefore be interpreted as bio-signal experiments with possible EEG/EMG mixtures.

### 3.2 Four causal second-order sections
The firmware processes every input sample through four cascaded sections. Each section keeps two persistent state values. Its recurrence can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}
w[n]&=x[n]-a_1w[n-1]-a_2w[n-2],\\
y[n]&=b_0w[n]+b_1w[n-1]+b_2w[n-2].
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
$$

For each section, the current output becomes the next section's input. Eight stored delays therefore carry the filter state across calls. The numerical coefficients are fixed in both inspected sender and IR-controller implementations. This is a causal IIR cascade, which introduces a frequency-dependent phase response. It does not implement forward/backward zero-phase filtering.

The sample rate matters to the physical frequency response. Reusing the same coefficients at a different cadence shifts the relationship between digital frequency and hertz. For that reason, the sampling discrepancy below belongs to the signal-processing interpretation, not just to the user interface.

### 3.3 Circular-buffer envelope and event threshold
The IR variant casts the filtered output to an integer, rectifies it, and maintains a 128-sample circular buffer with a running sum. Its integer envelope operation is

$$
\begin{aligned}
q[n]&=|\operatorname{int}(y[n])|,\\
e[n]&=4\left\lfloor\frac{1}{128}\sum_{k=0}^{127}q[n-k]\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
$$

Replacing the oldest sample makes each update constant work rather than recomputing the whole sum. Integer division occurs before multiplying by four. The controller tests $e[n]>13$, turns its LED on, and transmits on the first above-threshold event while the LED was previously off. It re-arms the transmitter after the envelope returns below the threshold. This implements an amplitude event detector with edge suppression, rather than a learned intent classifier.

### 3.4 Scheduling changes the effective history
The serial sender adds $10^6/500=2000$ microseconds to its timer. The archived IR controller adds $10^7/500=20000$ microseconds. Their nominal intervals are therefore 2 ms and 20 ms respectively, despite sharing a `SAMPLE_RATE` label of 500.

For a 128-sample history,

$$
T_{\mathrm{history}}=\frac{128}{f_s}.
\tag{4}
$$

The intended 500 Hz cadence corresponds to 0.256 seconds; a 50 Hz nominal cadence corresponds to 2.56 seconds. On a rising event, the IR code performs two transmissions with two blocking 200 ms delays, further disturbing sampling. A target interval is not a measured sampling-rate guarantee: ADC work, serial traffic, and blocking control operations must be included in timing measurements.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/algobrain/research/algobrain-software-styled.webp" width={1659} height={948} alt="Separate AlgoBrain serial analysis and archived envelope-triggered infrared control paths" caption="Figure 2. The upper branch targets 500 Hz serial acquisition. The archived control branch has a 20 ms timer and blocking transmission delays; the receiver re-arms after five seconds without a decoded IR frame." />

## Implementation
### 4.1 Serial ingestion and bounded plot buffers
The Python visualizer reads serial data on a background thread, parses the three-field packet, and puts tuples into a queue. A processing thread appends samples to 2500-element deques for raw signal, filtered signal, cycle, and display indices. At the assumed 500 Hz cadence, those bounded buffers retain approximately five seconds of history. The queue and session recording list are not bounded by the deque limit.

Waveform plots use the current buffer's sample indices. The CSV recorder adds a host timestamp and a manually selected event label. These labels support later comparison between an instructed action and its surrounding samples; the code does not train a model from them. Host reception timestamps also do not establish precise device acquisition times.

### 4.2 Windowed spectral inspection
Once 256 filtered samples are available, the visualizer takes the last 256, multiplies them by a Hann window, and computes an FFT. For $N=256$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
h[n]&=\tfrac12\!\left(1-\cos\frac{2\pi n}{N-1}\right),\\
X[k]&=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}h[n]y[n]e^{-j2\pi kn/N}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
$$

The interface displays positive-frequency magnitudes on a 0–50 Hz axis and marks conventional EEG frequency regions. Frequency bins assume 500 Hz, giving bin spacing $500/256\approx1.953$ Hz and a 0.512-second analysis window. These axes are valid only when the actual acquired cadence matches that assumption. The plot is an inspection tool, not evidence that each labeled band is neural activity.

The statistics panel's quantity named SNR uses filtered mean-square divided by filtered variance. It does not compare a separately identified clean signal with measured noise. This paper treats it as a software diagnostic rather than a calibrated signal-to-noise measurement.

### 4.3 IR receiver state and quiet-time suppression
The final receiver decodes IR frames, toggles its relay only when unblocked, and changes the red/green indicators. Every decoded frame updates `lastSignalTime`, including frames received while blocked. It releases the block only when the elapsed interval exceeds 5000 ms:

$$
t-t_{\mathrm{last\ decoded}}>5000\ \mathrm{ms}.
\tag{6}
$$

Repeated traffic can therefore extend the block: the receiver waits for a quiet interval rather than enforcing a fixed timeout from the first event. The specific-code comparison is commented out in the inspected file. The implemented path accepts decoded frames without that command check and provides no acknowledgement to the transmitter. The separation between transmitter and receiver makes each state machine inspectable, while delivery and command validation remain distinct engineering responsibilities.

## Evidence
### 5.1 Original hardware and project record
The gallery retains the original bio-amplifier/enclosure photograph, exhibition display, and competition documents. The project record reports fourth place among more than 150 teams at the national innovation competition in Rades. That recognition is separate from quantitative signal-classification performance.

The source archive establishes the implemented chain: custom analog hardware, acquisition and filtering firmware, a serial inspection client, event recording, and an IR/relay prototype. The new diagrams are source-derived explanations; their signals and spectral insets are illustrative. They do not add measured EEG recordings, clinical validation, classifier accuracy, or control latency.

### 5.2 Reproducible observations from the code
The inspected sender exposes its raw and filtered samples together, allowing a recorded input to be compared with the filter output. The fixed coefficients and persistent state make the digital operation reproducible. The timer constants, buffer lengths, threshold, repeated transmissions, and receiver block logic can each be inspected independently. This visibility is the useful foundation for synchronized hardware measurements and per-session evaluation.

## Discussion
AlgoBrain's technical value lies in connecting weak-signal hardware to observable embedded processing and a physical output. Keeping raw samples alongside filtered values and recording event labels makes failures investigable: drift, saturation, timing mismatch, artifacts, and threshold behavior can be examined rather than hidden behind a single control result.

A stronger evaluation would characterize the analog transfer response with known inputs, verify acquisition timestamps and jitter, and measure amplitude distributions across electrode placements and sessions. Artifact labeling should separate muscle, blink, movement, and contact events from the intended signal. Per-user calibration and explicit command validation would improve the control contract. Nonblocking transmission would make acquisition timing easier to maintain.

The current archive supports deterministic filtering and amplitude-triggered control. It does not support a claim that a waveform peak identifies a thought, that a spectral label proves an EEG source, or that this is a machine-learning project. The cover and figures therefore emphasize circuitry, signal processing, spectral analysis, and control state.

## References
1. **Primary acquisition firmware:** `Project Mind Controller/AlgoBrain/simple_data_sender.ino` — `loop`, `EEGFilter`, three-field serial output, and cycle markers in the supplied AlgoBrain archive.
2. **Desktop analysis:** `Project Mind Controller/AlgoBrain/algobrain_visualizer.py` — serial reader, queue processing, plot deques, Hann-window FFT, statistics, and CSV recording.
3. **IR controller:** `Project Mind Controller/codes/AlgoBrain_Code_v2__IR_led_Option_/AlgoBrain_Code_v2__IR_led_Option_.ino` — timer, `EMGFilter`, `getEnvelop`, rising-event logic, and repeated NEC transmissions.
4. **Receiver:** `Project Mind Controller/codes/final_reciver_AlgoBrain/final_reciver_AlgoBrain.ino` — relay toggle, status indicators, refreshed quiet timer, and commented command comparison.
5. **Hardware record:** project README, circuit/PCB archive, and original prototype/exhibition images. Documentation descriptions are distinguished from calibrated electrical measurements.

data.title: AquaFlow
data.summary: Fish-water monitoring with custom AC-based TDS sensing, ESP32 controls and a mobile dashboard.
data.paperTitle: A connected fish-water system with pulse-linked sensing and separated control state

projects.body:
## Abstract
AquaFlow connects a fish-water prototype, in-house conductivity-based sensing, an Arduino Nano measurement processor, an ESP32 network/controller layer, and a mobile monitoring interface. The supplied firmware implements a framed single-wire pulse handoff for TDS and temperature, local ultrasonic distance sensing, a freshness flag, and separate cloud ownership for measurements and requested relay states. The physical explanation relates feeding, recirculation, filtration, and water-quality interpretation. This paper distinguishes bulk ionic monitoring from ammonia-specific measurement and separates mineral adsorption from biological nitrification. The diagrams describe the prototype and inspected firmware without publishing proprietary sensing parameters or claiming unmeasured water-treatment performance.

**Keywords:** aquaculture monitoring; conductivity proxy; single-wire encoding; dual-core controller; state ownership; recirculation; filtration.

<ProjectAlbum />

## System specification
### 2.1 Physical loop and operating context
The evidence includes a tank test bench, controller enclosure, relay/sensor wiring, a system demonstration, and a mobile dashboard. A separate concept image explains a recirculating path from tank through pumping and filter media to aeration/return. The supplied folder also contains filter CAD and fish-feeder components named base, rotor, wall, and lid.

These artifacts establish the physical development work and functional water loop. A filter model does not establish a measured ammonia removal rate; feeder geometry does not establish an implemented feeding controller in the inspected ESP32 revision.

### 2.2 Embedded responsibilities
| Component | Inspected responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Arduino Nano | Acquire a TDS estimate and temperature; encode a sensor packet |
| One-wire handoff | Transfer framed pulse-width fields to the receiver |
| ESP32 local loop | Decode readings, assess sensor-link freshness and acquire distance |
| ESP32 cloud task | Publish sensor state, fetch desired relay state and handle connectivity |
| Relay layer | Apply pump, compressor and UV output choices |
| Mobile interface | Present readings, warnings, connection indicators and equipment controls |

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/aquaflow/research/recirculation-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Fish-water recirculation and equipment" caption="Figure 1. Functional water loop and controller/relay boundary, informed by the prototype and system concept. This figure does not report treatment efficacy." />

## Method
### 3.1 Feeding changes both solid and dissolved loads
Feed supports fish growth, while uneaten material and metabolic waste add loads to the water. Suspended material can be captured mechanically. Dissolved nitrogen requires a different interpretation: ammonium-binding mineral media and biological conversion have distinct mechanisms and operating dependencies.

Mineral adsorption depends on the material and water chemistry. Zeolite and bentonite have been studied for nitrogen-compound adsorption under aquaculture-relevant conditions; that background does not identify AquaFlow's exact filter material or establish its removal capacity. [Şahin et al., mineral adsorption study](https://www.academicoa.com/ILNS.71.34).

Biological filtration transforms ammonia through nitrite to nitrate rather than simply trapping it as a solid:

$$
\mathrm{NH_3/NH_4^+}\longrightarrow
\mathrm{NO_2^-}\longrightarrow\mathrm{NO_3^-}.
\tag{1}
$$

Biofilter operation and fish welfare also depend on oxygen and other water conditions. Temperature, pH, dissolved oxygen, nitrogen compounds, and species-specific needs therefore cannot be replaced by one TDS threshold. [FAO water-reuse and biological treatment background](https://www.fao.org/4/y5042e/y5042e07.htm).

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/aquaflow/research/feeding-filtration-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Feed load and filtration mechanisms" caption="Figure 2. Feeder CAD informs the component inset. Mechanical capture, mineral adsorption and biological nitrification address different loads; no removal rate is inferred." />

### 3.2 What the TDS path measures
AquaFlow reuses the in-house sensing foundation developed for Plantini. Its alternating measurement approach yields a conductivity-related response, interpreted through temperature context and calibration. In general,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\kappa_{25}&\approx\frac{\kappa_T}{1+\alpha(T-25)},\\
C_{\mathrm{TDS}}&\approx f_{\mathrm{solution}}\kappa_{25}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
$$

The conversion factor depends on ionic composition. TDS is useful as a bulk ionic trend and calibrated operating indicator; it is not a direct ammonia, dissolved-oxygen, or individual-contaminant measurement. Filtering solids, adsorbing ammonium, and changing dissolved salt composition may affect different measurements in different ways. [USGS specific-conductance background](https://water.usgs.gov/nwc/NWC/water_quality/tables/quality.abs.html).

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/aquaflow/research/conductivity-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Fish-water conductivity and measurement context" caption="Figure 3. Bulk ionic interpretation, temperature context and approximate TDS conversion. TDS does not identify ammonia or dissolved oxygen." />

### 3.3 Framed pulse communication
The supplied `nano.ino` and `esp.ino` pair use a one-wire pulse-width message, rather than UART or I²C. The semantic order is a start marker, TDS field, separator, temperature field, and end marker. The receiver checks timing boundaries and waits for the required transitions before decoding the two values.

The public figure preserves field order and receiver responsibilities, but omits pin assignments, pulse constants, sensing circuitry and calibration coefficients. The transport should not be described as checksum-protected or acknowledged: those guarantees are not implemented in the inspected path.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/aquaflow/research/controller-link-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Nano to ESP32 pulse communication" caption="Figure 4. Source-derived single-wire field order, receiver responsibilities and five-second sensor-link freshness boundary. Pulse widths are schematic." />

## Implementation
### 4.1 Local sensing and freshness
The ESP32's main loop receives Nano packets and measures ultrasonic distance. Accepted packets update the retained TDS and temperature values and record the last packet time. Let $n_r$ count accepted packets and $\Delta t=t-t_{\mathrm{last}}$ denote their age. The Nano-link flag $a_N$ becomes false after more than five seconds without an accepted packet:

$$
a_N(t)=\mathbf{1}[n_r>0]\,\mathbf{1}[\Delta t\le5\ \mathrm s].
\tag{3}
$$

The stored numeric readings remain available after link loss. The freshness flag must accompany them; a retained value alone should not be presented as a newly measured state. Invalid ultrasonic readings are published as unavailable rather than as a physical distance.

### 4.2 Two execution contexts
The networking task is pinned to core 0, while the local sensor loop runs on core 1. A critical section protects snapshots of the shared measurement values. This isolates responsibilities and avoids holding that lock through an HTTP request; it does not establish hard real-time behavior or eliminate every timing interaction.

The cloud task targets sensor publication and relay polling at approximately one-second intervals. HTTP duration, reconnects, task scheduling and local acquisition add delay. This interval is a configured cadence, not a measured end-to-end latency guarantee.

### 4.3 Separate measurement and command ownership
The author describes the applications as Firebase-connected. The supplied ESP32 revision implements that cloud boundary through Firestore REST: it PATCHes a sensor document and GETs a separate relay document. Its data flow is therefore specified from the actual firmware, rather than inferred as a Realtime Database stream or MQTT subscriber.

The separation addresses an explicit source comment about overwritten app changes. The device publishes measurements and listens for requested pump, compressor and UV states; it does not continually republish its old relay choices over the user's desired state. Changed cloud choices trigger local relay application.

Boot initializes relay outputs off, then fetches stored choices if connected. On a later cloud failure, the inspected polling function returns without applying a new state. It does not provide a documented per-command acknowledgement, automatic stale-command shutdown, or verified actuator feedback. Desired state and observed hardware state must therefore remain distinct concepts.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/aquaflow/research/live-telemetry-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="ESP32 cloud state ownership" caption="Figure 5. Local sensing and networking responsibilities, sensor publication and requested relay states. The inspected revision uses Firestore REST with a configured one-second cadence." />

## Evidence
The existing dashboard displays temperature, TDS, water-level status, warnings, pump/compressor controls and separate connection badges. Its captured state shows a Firebase-connected badge alongside a disconnected MQTT badge. These are independent visible interface indicators; the supplied ESP32 file establishes the Firestore HTTP path, while the screenshot alone does not establish a working MQTT transport.

The existing tank, wiring, enclosure and demonstration remain in the gallery. The supplied filter and feeder CAD inform the physical explanation. New diagrams show the recirculating loop, feed/waste/filter mechanisms, conductivity interpretation, pulse handoff, and cloud state ownership. They do not invent treatment measurements, fish-growth outcomes, or an implemented AI feeding policy from interface labels.

## Discussion
The most substantial software decision is ownership: measurement state flows outward from the device, while desired actuator choices flow inward from the shared cloud state. Separating those paths avoids a common feedback race in which a device overwrites a fresh operator command with its previous local state.

The next evaluation layer would measure packet acceptance, link-loss behavior, cloud-to-output delay and actual output feedback over a recorded run. On the water side, nutrient/contaminant-specific testing, filter loading, oxygen availability and feeding load matter alongside bulk TDS trends. The prototype makes sensing and equipment operation visible; its performance should be assessed against those distinct physical and communication requirements.

## References
- Owner-supplied controller revision: `codeTDS/nano/esp/esp.ino`; Nano sender: `codeTDS/nano/nano.ino`. Inspected read-only; network credentials and private implementation parameters are not published.
- Hardware source record: filter CAD, feeder base/rotor/wall/lid models, and existing tank/controller/wiring media retained in the project gallery.
- In-house TDS research and supplied sensor firmware, shared with the Plantini sensing foundation; public discussion limited to operating principles and interface responsibilities.
- [USGS water-quality measurement principles](https://water.usgs.gov/nwc/NWC/water_quality/tables/quality.abs.html).
- [FAO: water reuse and biological treatment](https://www.fao.org/4/y5042e/y5042e07.htm).
- [Şahin et al. (2018): natural-mineral adsorption of nitrogen compounds](https://www.academicoa.com/ILNS.71.34).

data.title: Cleanoov
data.summary: A thermal-inspection interface for locating possible solar-panel hotspots.

projects.body:
## Problem
Solar installations are large, repetitive, and difficult to inspect panel by panel. A thermal camera can turn temperature differences into a visible pattern, but that is only the start of the job. Reflections, hot surroundings, junctions, and image texture can all create bright regions that look important at first glance.

The useful outcome is not simply a colourful thermal frame. It is a short, reviewable list of locations that may need a technician to inspect.

## What I built
Cleanoov brings that review process into a focused thermal hotspot detector. The recorded interface accepts a video file or a live stream, displays the thermal image, draws candidate boxes, and reports the number of current candidates.

The controls expose the decisions that change a detector's behaviour: sensitivity, the largest permitted box as a percentage of the frame, minimum spot size, texture filtering, and a cluster filter. That makes the tool an inspection aid with visible tuning controls rather than a black box that silently decides what is faulty.

The project also includes a solar-cleaning robot render. It is a concept for the operational side of the wider idea, not evidence of a tested autonomous robot.

## How it works
### Start from thermal contrast, then constrain the result
The interface starts by identifying bright thermal regions relative to the rest of the frame. Raising sensitivity restricts the candidates to hotter regions; lowering it can reveal weaker temperature differences but also introduces more noise. A field workflow needs both settings because a threshold that works at one time of day or with one camera palette may fail elsewhere.

### Reject shapes that do not fit the inspection task
A fault candidate should have a plausible size in the image. The maximum-box control can discard very large warm areas, such as a whole roof zone, while the minimum-spot control removes tiny isolated pixels. These are practical safeguards: without them, a detector can spend its time reporting things that are either too broad to localise or too small to investigate.

### Use texture and density as evidence, not as a verdict
Thermal images contain texture from module boundaries, ground, reflections, and compression. The texture filter offers a way to suppress candidates that do not have the local variation expected by the chosen settings. The cluster filter addresses another failure mode: many overlapping boxes can turn one confusing region into a long list of alerts. Grouping or suppressing dense clusters makes the overlay easier to read.

These controls are only a first pass. A box is a candidate for inspection, not a confirmed electrical fault. Confirmation needs context such as panel layout, irradiance, camera calibration, repeat observations, and where appropriate an electrical measurement.

## Result
The supplied evidence shows a working inspection interface with video and stream controls, adjustable filters, and hotspot overlays on a solar-array thermal frame. It demonstrates the review workflow and the kinds of false positives the controls are intended to manage.

It does not establish detection accuracy, camera calibration, fault-classification performance, or robot field performance. Those require labelled thermal data and on-site validation.

## What I would improve
I would add a frame-by-frame review queue that keeps the source timestamp, panel-row position, detector settings, and an operator decision for every alert. Requiring a candidate to persist across adjacent frames would reduce one-frame noise. A calibration and validation plan should compare the alerts with confirmed field findings, then report precision and missed defects separately for different weather conditions.

For the robot concept, the next concrete milestone is a safe manual or supervised platform test: traction, panel-safe contact forces, water use, obstacle handling, and an emergency-stop path all need evidence before autonomy becomes a meaningful claim.

data.title: Cyclops
data.summary: A staged research engine turning a clarified question into organized web and paper evidence.

projects.body:
## Problem
Deep research fails in several ways before writing begins. The question may be too vague, results may repeat the same source, a paper may be unavailable, or a PDF may hide important information inside figures and tables.

Cyclops treats research as a sequence of evidence-processing tasks. Its goal is to turn an initial question into a clearer brief, collect relevant web and academic material, and produce organized reports that retain connections to their sources.

## What I built
I built a Python workflow with separate stages for interviewing the user, generating queries, collecting sources, removing duplicates, downloading documents, extracting information, and writing reports. The implementation is private; this article focuses on its behavior and architecture.

The supplied cover is a concept overview. The reviewed implementation is a staged research pipeline, so the illustrated interface and feature labels should not be treated as proof that every depicted screen is implemented.

## How it works
### Start with a research brief
The opening stage collects research intent and source preferences. Query generation expands the brief into searches appropriate to the topic. Later analysis uses that intent and its relevance criteria when deciding which information is useful.

Finding a document and finding an answer are different tasks. A broadly related paper may appear in search results without supporting the specific question being investigated.

### Process papers and web pages differently
The academic path discovers paper links, removes repeated results, resolves document locations, and downloads PDFs. An additional search path looks for alternative document sources when the first route is insufficient. Another deduplication pass limits repeated work across sources.

PDF analysis goes beyond treating a document as one plain text block. The implementation examines page complexity and includes paths for text extraction, tables, OCR, and rendered page images. Complex pages can be processed differently from ordinary text pages, preserving information a text-only pass may overlook.

The web path collects URLs, deduplicates them, and retrieves content through browser workers. Saved pages are analyzed in batches before their results are assembled into a web report. Keeping the paths separate lets the extraction method match the material.

### Make intermediate work visible
Query lists, filtered URLs, extracted content, and analysis outputs are saved between stages. These artifacts help locate where a weak result began: discovery, download, extraction, relevance filtering, or synthesis.

The sequence runner executes stages in order and stops when a stage fails or a required script is missing. This prevents downstream work after an explicit process failure. It is still a simple runner, rather than a durable workflow service with automatic resumption and versioned checkpoints.

### Preserve a route back to evidence
Paper analysis records relevance information and produces structured summaries. The academic report combines summaries with references to retained local PDFs, while the web report follows its own collected material. Document links give the reader a route back to evidence, although links alone do not prove that each sentence is supported.

The reviewed folder contains academic and web report stages. A combined final PDF and video-research path appear in planning notes, so they are not presented here as completed outputs of this runner.

## Result
Cyclops connects question clarification, source collection, document processing, and report generation in one inspectable workflow. Its useful design idea is separating research into stages with visible inputs and outputs: a report can be improved by fixing the evidence pipeline that produced it.

The local implementation includes generated reports and intermediate analysis artifacts. No research-quality score or execution benchmark is claimed here, and private source code is not distributed with the portfolio.

## What I would improve
I would add a run manifest recording input hashes, completed stages, output locations, and failures. That would allow a failed extraction to resume without repeating successful downloads and prevent stale artifacts from entering a new report.

Citation validation should connect important statements to specific pages or passages, with uncertain findings visibly marked. URL normalization also needs care: removing all query parameters can merge genuinely different documents. A stronger pipeline would retain original URLs, use source-aware canonicalization, and compare downloaded content hashes before deciding two sources are identical.

data.title: EasyShield
data.summary: A complete face anti-spoofing pipeline, from dataset preparation to live testing.
data.paperTitle: A visual liveness gate: dataset engineering, inference, and decision semantics

projects.body:
## Abstract
EasyShield is a face presentation-attack detection pipeline developed as a liveness gate for identity recognition. Its contribution includes the data-production tools and inspection interfaces surrounding a YOLOv12-nano model: face extraction, augmentation, curation, detection-label generation, training, and live evaluation. The source implements two execution paths: continuous Windows inference and a five-frame Linux scan with confidence filtering and majority aggregation. This paper specifies the crop-to-decision contract, distinguishes offline and live face localization, and examines the class-mapping assumptions that connect training labels to deployment. The repository reports 92.30% accuracy on an 8,000-image comparison; these are published project results, rather than a new benchmark run for this page.

**Keywords:** presentation-attack detection; liveness; dataset curation; edge inference; decision thresholds; YOLO.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/easyshield/easyshield-thumbnail.webp" width={1600} height={900} alt="Preserved original EasyShield face anti-spoofing project artwork" caption="Original project overview artwork. Its displayed statistics refer to the repository report discussed in Evidence." />

### Development documented in practice
The album below records the development workstation, training output, dataset inspection, and live presentation-attack tests. These original photographs, screenshots, and demonstration videos show the project being built and tested. Select a thumbnail to inspect it; View more reveals the complete album.

<ProjectAlbum />

## System specification
### 2.1 Liveness before identity
A face detector locates a candidate region. The liveness model then evaluates evidence of a real face or a presentation attack in that region and its surrounding context. Identity recognition is a separate downstream responsibility in [NiotoShield](/projects/niotoshield). A liveness score alone does not establish a person's identity.

The implementation uses detection-style YOLO outputs: bounding-box classes and confidence values from `result.boxes`, rather than a classification-head probability vector. A cropped region is therefore converted into a binary liveness decision by interpreting the detector's returned class and score.

| Layer | Input | Responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Offline preparation | Images and videos | Extract and curate face-centered samples |
| Dataset packaging | Curated real / fake images | Generate normalized boxes and a train / validation / test split |
| Live localization | Camera frames | Locate faces with an OpenCV Haar cascade |
| Liveness model | Resized contextual crop | Return detection classes and confidence |
| Decision interface | Accepted predictions | Display real / attack evidence and scan aggregation |

### 2.2 Contextual cropping
The live model receives more than a tightly cut face. The code expands a detected face box by padding proportional to its width, clips the crop to the camera frame, and resizes it to $640\times640$. Context can retain useful evidence of a screen, printed sheet, or presentation boundary. The displayed rectangle uses a different, smaller padding; it should not be confused with the actual model input.

For face box $(x,y,w,h)$ in a frame of width $W$ and height $H$, the model crop is defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}
p&=\lfloor1.5w\rfloor,\\
x_1&=\max(0,x-p),\quad x_2=\min(W,x+w+p),\\
y_1&=\max(0,y-p),\quad y_2=\min(H,y+h+p).
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
$$

Clipping handles faces near the frame edge. Resizing standardizes the tensor dimensions; it does not guarantee that each original crop has the same aspect ratio or amount of background.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/easyshield/research/liveness-gate-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Live contextual liveness pipeline" caption="Figure 1. Camera localization, contextual crop, detection outputs and semantic liveness decision. Identity recognition remains a downstream responsibility." />

## Method
### 3.1 Constructing a usable training set
The face-extraction tool uses MTCNN to obtain samples from photographs and video. Augmentation changes rotation, blur, brightness, contrast, and orientation. The filtering interface supports automatic face checks together with manual review, backup, and undo operations. These are separate stages: augmentation expands appearance variation, while curation determines whether a sample remains useful and correctly labeled.

The dataset preparation script uses an OpenCV DNN face detector to produce YOLO-format box labels. It shuffles the image collection and allocates 80% to training, 10% to validation, and 10% to testing. Each label contains a class and normalized box center, width, and height. This is an image-level split; evaluation of unseen identities, cameras, or recording sessions requires explicit grouping beyond the current random split.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/easyshield/research/dataset-workflow-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Offline liveness dataset workflow" caption="Figure 2. Source-derived extraction, augmentation, curation, box-label generation and training, with the current 80/10/10 image split." />

### 3.2 Offline and live localization
MTCNN belongs to the extraction and filtering tools. The live Windows and Linux testers use a Haar cascade. The Windows path localizes faces at reduced frame resolution and maps coordinates back to the original frame. Face detections can be reused between localization steps, while the liveness model evaluates the contextual crops.

This separation keeps dataset production and interactive inference independently inspectable. It also creates a distribution boundary: the regions produced by offline tools and live localization may differ in framing, scale, and background. Crop consistency should therefore be evaluated alongside model accuracy.

### 3.3 Five-frame decision aggregation
The Linux tester collects up to five face crops, discards predictions below its selected confidence threshold, and counts the remaining real and fake outcomes. A scan reports real only when the real count strictly exceeds the fake count:

$$
\begin{aligned}
n_R&=\sum_{k\in\mathcal A}\mathbf{1}[\hat c_k=R],\\
n_F&=\sum_{k\in\mathcal A}\mathbf{1}[\hat c_k=F],\\
\hat d&=\begin{cases}R,&n_R>n_F,\\F,&n_R\le n_F.\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
$$

Here $\mathcal A$ is the set of accepted crop predictions after confidence filtering. Ties and a scan with no accepted model outcomes follow the attack branch. A missing face or failed capture can also produce a separate interface error before aggregation. Average confidence is a displayed diagnostic, not a calibrated probability that authentication is safe.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/easyshield/research/decision-contract-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Five-frame scan and class mapping" caption="Figure 3. Linux confidence-filtered aggregation and the differing class-ID assumptions across dataset and live scripts. Checkpoint metadata establishes the deployment meaning." />

## Implementation
### 4.1 Training and inspection tools
The trainer exposes epochs, batch size, optimizer, learning rate, worker count, caching, and device selection in a GUI. It invokes Ultralytics training and provides access to saved run artifacts. The surrounding tools make intermediate products visible: extracted faces, edited datasets, labels, training output, and live predictions can each be reviewed separately.

The Windows tester supports continuous camera/file evaluation with overlays. The Linux tester adds an explicit scan action and aggregation result, making the decision boundary visible to the operator rather than hiding it inside a frame loop.

### 4.2 The class-map contract
The inspected revision contains a material integration detail: dataset preparation and the benchmark use the ordering `0 = fake, 1 = real`, while the live testers interpret `0 = real, 1 = fake`. A deployed checkpoint must be paired with its actual saved class metadata. Numeric IDs cannot be treated as universal semantics across these scripts.

This paper and its diagrams use semantic labels **real** and **fake**. Verifying the checkpoint's class mapping is necessary before connecting liveness output to an identity gate. The original repository has been inspected without changing its training or inference code.

## Evidence
### 5.1 Repository-reported evaluation
The README reports the following results for its 8,000-image comparison. The table preserves that provenance; it does not imply an independently repeated experiment or a verified edge-device latency measurement.

| Metric | Repository-reported value |
| --- | --- |
| Accuracy | 92.30% |
| F1 | 92.68% |
| Attack presentation classification error | 6.25% |
| Bona fide presentation classification error | 2.50% |
| Average classification error | 4.38% |

The error-rate relationship is

$$
\mathrm{ACER}=\frac{\mathrm{APCER}+\mathrm{BPCER}}{2}.
\tag{3}
$$

These quantities distinguish attacks accepted as bona fide from bona fide presentations rejected as attacks. Their interpretation depends on the positive-class convention, threshold, and evaluation protocol. The benchmark script computes several metrics, but its score construction and class mapping require review before treating ROC/AUC outputs as fully validated.

### 5.2 Interface and artifact record
The existing demonstration montage, face-extraction screens, trainer interfaces, dataset/prediction views, and live test screenshots are retained in the project gallery. They document the workflow and its inspectable outputs. Architecture figures describe the source implementation; they do not add measured accuracy or substitute for a held-out evaluation.

## Discussion
The engineering strength is the complete route from raw footage to an inspectable liveness decision. Dataset tools expose quality issues early, contextual crops retain presentation evidence, and scan aggregation makes repeated observations explicit. The highest-value evaluation extensions are identity/session-disjoint splits, threshold sweeps with consistent class semantics, and device-specific latency measured across capture, localization, preprocessing, and inference.

A strong comparison also needs attack coverage beyond the training collection, including previously unseen presentation media and camera conditions. The reported result establishes a project evaluation record; it does not establish universal attack resistance or state-of-the-art status across protocols.

## References
The implementation analysis uses revision `3afb0fe760e3d57b3a7d3e78d0977ebb9abce1de` of [EasyShield v2.5](https://github.com/mahostar/EasyShield_v2.5).

- [Dataset preparation and label generation](https://github.com/mahostar/EasyShield_v2.5/blob/3afb0fe760e3d57b3a7d3e78d0977ebb9abce1de/dataset%20preparing%20tools/prepare_data.py).
- [Windows live tester](https://github.com/mahostar/EasyShield_v2.5/blob/3afb0fe760e3d57b3a7d3e78d0977ebb9abce1de/Testing%20Code%20%28windows%29/test_model.py).
- [Linux five-frame scan](https://github.com/mahostar/EasyShield_v2.5/blob/3afb0fe760e3d57b3a7d3e78d0977ebb9abce1de/Testing%20Code%20%28Linux%29/Raspberry_Pi4_Custom_pipeline_testing_tool.py).
- [Evaluation script](https://github.com/mahostar/EasyShield_v2.5/blob/3afb0fe760e3d57b3a7d3e78d0977ebb9abce1de/Trained%20TOOL%20for%20YOLO/model_benchmark.py) and [reported comparison](https://github.com/mahostar/EasyShield_v2.5/blob/3afb0fe760e3d57b3a7d3e78d0977ebb9abce1de/README.md).

data.title: EazyCode
data.summary: A training platform connecting course discovery, enrollment, and learner schedules.

projects.body: ## Problem Publishing a course catalogue is only the beginning of running a training platform. The harder work starts when a learner enrolls in several courses, an administrator changes their access, or two live sessions compete for the same person's time. EazyCode connects these workflows for a technology training platform in Tunisia. Its public catalogue covers AI, cloud computing, web development, cybersecurity, and certification-oriented training. The engineering challenge is keeping the catalogue, enrollment records, and learning spaces consistent as the programme changes. ## What I built The application combines a React and Vite frontend, React Router navigation, Firestore-backed course and enrollment data, and separate administration, learner, and trainer experiences. Course detail and account pages load through lazy imports, with a shared loading fallback rather than loading every dashboard with the landing page. Beyond the public site, the implementation includes configurable enrollment questions, coupon pricing, participant management, course scheduling, and enrollment email integration. The repository is private; this case study describes the architecture without distributing its source. ## How it works ### Treat enrollment as a relationship One of the most useful design decisions is matching enrollment records by course ID first, while retaining title matching for older records. A stable identifier survives a course rename; the compatibility path lets older data remain usable during migration. Account updates reconcile the learner's selected courses against existing enrollment rows. The process keeps and updates a matching row, creates a row for a newly selected course, and removes rows no longer represented in the selection. It also normalizes email addresses before matching them. This is more deliberate than appending another enrollment whenever an administrator saves an account. The important lesson is that reconciliation is a desired-state operation: the selected course set describes what should exist. The current implementation performs multiple Firestore operations, so the algorithm itself does not guarantee an atomic update. ### Make flexible forms predictable Enrollment questions are represented as field definitions with stable IDs, types, and required flags. The validator handles required checkboxes separately from text-like values, so a required consent-style answer cannot pass merely because a field exists. The same definitions feed a structured WhatsApp handoff message, including the course, price information, and additional responses. Pricing distinguishes percentage discounts from fixed reductions and clamps the final price at zero. These small boundaries matter: form configuration and promotion rules should remain understandable to administrators without becoming scattered UI conditions. ### Check the learner's whole schedule Scheduling checks combine account course assignments with enrollment-derived course IDs. This catches a learner whose relationship to a course exists in either representation. Session intervals include a default 15-minute gap, and conflict checks can exclude the session currently being edited. For example, a two-hour session beginning at 10:00 conflicts with another beginning at 12:10 because the transition window is still active. The overlap comparison uses strict inequalities, so an exact 15-minute boundary is allowed. Locally entered date-time values are converted to ISO timestamps before storage; consistent time-zone handling remains an important design consideration. ### Keep email transport separate The Cloudflare request handler delegates enrollment email work to a shared server module and translates failures into HTTP responses. Separating the handler from message construction makes it easier to keep deployment adapters thin and evolve the email workflow without duplicating the whole application. ## Result [EazyCode is available online](https://eazycodeacademy.com). The implementation goes beyond course presentation: it links enrollment configuration, account-course reconciliation, scheduling, and communication in one platform. The useful engineering takeaway is that education software is largely a consistency problem. A polished catalogue helps someone choose a course; stable relationships and predictable updates help the team deliver it. No enrollment, conversion, or email-delivery metrics are claimed here. ## What I would improve I would make enrollment reconciliation transactional or move it behind an authoritative server operation, then test retries and simultaneous account edits. Scheduling should use an explicit academy time zone and test daylight-saving transitions for international learners. Email delivery would benefit from idempotency keys and recorded delivery state so a retry cannot silently send duplicate messages. For a growing catalogue, I would also replace collection-wide matching with indexed queries and introduce a clear migration path that eventually retires title-based enrollment matching.

data.title: FabricLens
data.paperTitle: Textile defect localization with staged detector adaptation
data.summary: Staged YOLO adaptation, annotated textile detections, and a threaded CPU inspection interface.

projects.body:
## Abstract
This paper documents a single-class textile defect localization pipeline built around YOLO11s. The implementation connects image/label preparation, frozen-backbone adaptation, full-model fine-tuning, checkpoint selection, batch inference, and a desktop inspection interface. Saved annotated images, learning curves, and a confusion matrix provide experiment artifacts for visual review. The viewer separates its event loop from CPU inference through a background thread and per-image result caching. The engineering contribution is an inspectable path from dataset contract to localized predictions; the available artifacts do not establish deployment performance across textile conditions.

**Keywords:** textile inspection; object detection; transfer learning; normalized annotations; CPU inference; visual review.

<ProjectAlbum />

## System specification
### 2.1 Detection task and annotation contract
Given a textile image $I$, the detector returns candidate regions $\{(b_i,q_i)\}$, where $b_i$ is a bounding box and $q_i$ is its confidence score. The dataset uses a single defect class. Labels encode the class identifier and normalized box geometry:

$$
\mathbf{b} = \left(\frac{x_c}{W},\;\frac{y_c}{H},\;\frac{w}{W},\;\frac{h}{H}\right).
\tag{1}
$$

Here $W$ and $H$ are image dimensions, $(x_c,y_c)$ is the box center, and $w,h$ are its width and height in pixels. Clean examples have empty label files. Image/label pairing, class consistency, and the inclusion of clean frames define the supervision boundary [1].

### 2.2 Pipeline components
| Component | Responsibility | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dataset preparation | Acquire and organize image/label pairs | Training directory structure |
| Staged training | Adapt the head, then fine-tune the model | Selected checkpoints |
| Batch inference | Apply thresholds and draw predicted boxes | Annotated JPEG files |
| Inspection viewer | Browse images and cached CPU predictions | Reviewable image display |

Small defects compete with weave, seams, folds, and lighting variations. The interface therefore retains spatial annotations rather than reducing an image to a single quality verdict.

## Method
### 3.1 Staged detector adaptation
Training starts from YOLO11s. The first stage freezes backbone layers 0–9 while adapting the remaining trainable layers. The second stage loads the selected first-stage checkpoint and unfreezes the model with a lower initial learning rate [2]. Both stages use 640-pixel input resolution, batch size 16, and four data-loading workers. These are configured parameters, rather than claims that one setting is optimal for all fabrics.

Mosaic augmentation is enabled in both stages. Mixup is disabled during initial adaptation and set to 0.05 during full fine-tuning. Early stopping and periodic checkpoint saving support recoverable experiments. The selected weights, image resolution, augmentation configuration, and dataset partition together determine the meaning of an evaluation.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/projects/fabric-training-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Textile labels and two-stage detector adaptation" caption="Figure 1. Image/label supervision, frozen-backbone adaptation, full-model fine-tuning and selected weights. Fabric scenes are schematic; the settings follow train.py." />

### 3.2 Confidence filtering and overlap suppression
Batch inference uses confidence threshold $\tau_q=0.25$ and non-maximum-suppression IoU threshold $\tau_{\mathrm{IoU}}=0.45$ [3]. The overlap measure between candidate boxes $A$ and $B$ is

$$
\operatorname{IoU}(A,B)=\frac{|A\cap B|}{|A\cup B|}.
\tag{2}
$$

The inference library applies the configured thresholds, after which the runner records detection counts and the highest score per image, plots retained predictions, and saves annotated outputs. A confidence score is a model score; calibration would be required to interpret it as a probability of physical defect.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/projects/fabric-detection-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Confidence filtering and overlap suppression for textile defect boxes" caption="Figure 2. Candidate boxes become inspectable defect locations through confidence filtering and NMS. The pictured fabric and scores are schematic examples, not measured predictions." />

### 3.3 Checkpoint and input resolution
The runner searches full-training selected weights, full-training final weights, frozen-stage selected weights, and frozen-stage final weights in that order. It searches test images before validation images. This fallback behavior enables inspection when some expected artifacts are absent, but the actual checkpoint and source partition must be recorded before using a result in a benchmark.

## Implementation
### 4.1 Batch inspection artifacts
The batch runner writes images under the saved inference-results directory. Each output preserves the original scene and overlays the detector's predicted regions. The gallery contains existing examples with narrow anomalies, elongated regions, and multiple boxes. No new model inference was performed to produce these portfolio images.

### 4.2 Threaded desktop inspection
<ProjectFigure src="/images/projects/fabric-viewer-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Textile viewer cache and background CPU inference flow" caption="Figure 3. Cache hits reuse predictions; misses launch a CPU worker, retain computed boxes and update the display while the main event loop continues. Interface images are schematic." />

The inspected Tkinter viewer loads its model on the CPU and runs inference in a background thread. Results are cached by image path so redraws can reuse existing predictions. Image navigation, fullscreen display, and keyboard exit operate through the interface event loop [4]. This separation avoids repeating inference on every display frame; responsiveness under sustained use requires runtime measurement.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/fabric-inspection/viewer-preview.webp" width={1392} height={829} alt="Textile inspection interface reconstruction" caption="Figure 4. Lightweight reconstruction of the inspection interface showing an existing annotated output. The preview does not execute YOLO or load the ML environment." />

The screenshot companion uses a standard-library Python web server to display a browser reconstruction from optimized saved media. It does not import the viewer's automatic dependency installer or execute the inference runner. Original project files remain untouched.

## Evidence
The visible album above contains saved project detections, training curves, and a confusion matrix. The viewer preview is explicitly marked as a reconstruction; the cover is concept artwork.

Annotated outputs provide qualitative evidence of localization behavior. Learning curves and the confusion matrix document a saved experiment. A controlled evaluation would additionally require the dataset manifest, held-out labels, checkpoint identity, inference thresholds, and metric calculation procedure. No factory deployment result or cross-fabric accuracy claim is inferred from these images.

## Discussion
### 6.1 Evaluation design
Evaluation should be stratified by fabric type, lighting, defect size, and difficult negative examples such as seams or folds. Separate review of false positives and missed defects is needed across confidence thresholds. Resizing deserves explicit analysis: a narrow defect visible at native resolution can occupy very few pixels after model preprocessing.

Image-level splits should also account for near-duplicate frames and shared source material. A documented held-out set makes later changes in augmentation, adaptation strategy, and suppression thresholds comparable.

### 6.2 Viewer state and reproducibility
The interface should distinguish pending inference from a completed result containing zero detections. Background results must update only the image they belong to. Bounded prefetch and cache eviction would support longer inspection sessions while keeping memory predictable.

An exported inspection result should retain checkpoint identity, input resolution, thresholds, source-image identity, and prediction metadata. These additions would make a visual artifact reproducible and allow later comparison against revised model weights.

The implemented pipeline separates preparation, adaptation, inference, and review. Its value lies in making localized predictions accessible for inspection while preserving the conditions under which they were generated.

## References
1. **Dataset preparation:** the project's acquisition and organization scripts — image/label pairing, normalized single-class annotations, and clean samples.
2. **Detector training:** `train.py` — YOLO11s initialization, backbone freezing, checkpoint handoff, full-model fine-tuning, and augmentation configuration.
3. **Batch inference:** `inference.py` — ordered checkpoint lookup, input-directory fallback, confidence/IoU settings, and annotated exports.
4. **Desktop inspection:** `final/infrencer.py` — Tkinter event loop, CPU model execution, background thread, and per-image cache.
5. **Experiment artifacts:** saved inference results and the full-training run's learning curves and confusion matrix.

data.title: Faza3D
data.summary: A 3D-printing storefront that separates ready-to-order products from custom fabrication requests.

projects.body:
## Problem
A small 3D-printing service has two very different order types. Ready-made products should be simple to browse and order. Custom jobs need enough information to decide whether a model can be made, how much material it needs, how long it may take, and what the customer actually wants.

Treating both paths as one generic contact form hides the manufacturing decisions from the customer and creates unnecessary back-and-forth for the maker.

## What I built
Faza3D is a React storefront with a catalogue, a custom-print route, a protected admin route, and theme preferences stored in the browser. The catalogue presents a fixed set of product cards with a material weight, price, product description, and an order link to Messenger.

The custom-print screen accepts either a model file or a model link, collects colour, infill, contact details, and notes, then shows an immediate planning estimate. It accepts common fabrication inputs including STL, OBJ, 3MF, STEP, and STP. The supplied gallery also documents the physical side of the service: finished prints and multiple printer setups.

## How it works
### Keep catalogue checkout lightweight
The catalogue is deliberately direct. Product information is defined in the frontend, and each card sends the buyer to the same Messenger ordering channel. That can be a reasonable early operating model: customers ask questions in a familiar channel and the maker can confirm stock, colour, and delivery before accepting an order.

It also exposes the limit of the current approach. Stock, orders, payments, and fulfilment status are not modelled as a transactional storefront, so Messenger is the handoff point rather than an integrated checkout.

### Ask for fabrication inputs before estimating
Custom printing needs more than a picture. The order form asks where the model comes from, the requested colour, infill, and notes. The source uses selected file size as a temporary stand-in for part weight, or a default weight for a linked model. It then combines a setup cost, an estimated material cost, an infill multiplier, and an estimated print-time charge.

That is useful as an expectation-setting estimate, but it is not a slicer result. File size does not reliably describe the geometry, wall count, support requirement, material volume, or print time. The interface should label this distinction clearly so a customer understands that the final quote follows model review.

### Make visual preference persistent without making it account data
The theme switcher stores light/dark mode and the selected visual style in local storage. This makes the experience feel consistent for a returning visitor without requiring authentication or sending a preference to a server.

The project includes Firebase dependencies and an admin route, but the reviewed custom-order flow currently simulates a successful submission in the browser. The source reviewed here does not show a file upload or an order record being written to a backend.

## Result
Faza3D demonstrates a useful separation between standard products and custom fabrication. The gallery supports both parts of the story: a public-facing shop interface and real printing equipment and outputs.

The custom-order estimate is a frontend planning aid, not a confirmed quote, and the submitted request is not yet persisted by the reviewed code. Those boundaries matter because manufacturing promises should come from geometry and machine planning, not from a polished form alone.

## What I would improve
I would move models to private object storage, run a server-side parser for supported formats, and derive the quote from slicer output: filament volume, chosen material, layer height, support material, machine profile, and estimated duration. Each request should receive a status trail from intake through review, quote approval, printing, quality check, and delivery.

For the catalogue, the next step is inventory and order data with a proper payment or confirmed-order state. The existing Messenger handoff can remain useful for questions, but it should not be the only record of a job once the service handles more than a small number of orders.

data.title: MoviNight
data.summary: A Rust and Tauri movie explorer with filtered discovery and locally saved watchlists.

projects.body:
## Problem
Finding something to watch involves two different tasks: exploring a catalogue and remembering what caught your attention. A discovery app becomes more useful when browsing, trailers, a watchlist, and viewing history share one interface.

MoviNight puts those tasks in a desktop application. Catalogue data comes from TMDB, while the user's watchlist and watched history remain in local files. That distinction matters: local persistence removes the need for an account-based list service, but discovery and embedded trailers still depend on network services.

## What I built
The application uses a vanilla JavaScript interface inside Tauri v2, with Rust commands handling API calls and persistence. It supports movie and television discovery, title search, genre and language filters, streaming-provider selection, detail views, and YouTube trailers.

### See the application in motion

<video src="/images/projects/movinight-demo.mp4" poster="/images/projects/movinight-demo-poster.webp" aria-label="Animated MoviNight application demonstration from the project repository" width="1332" height="720" controls loop muted playsInline preload="none" style={{ width: "100%", height: "auto" }} />

The source review follows the shipped frontend in `dist/main.js` and the backend in `src-tauri/src/lib.rs`. These files show the actual command boundary and data model more precisely than the README's feature list.

## How it works
### Keep the webview-to-Rust boundary explicit
The frontend calls named Tauri commands through `invoke`. Rust deserializes TMDB responses into separate movie and TV structures, including optional poster paths and different title and release-date fields. A generic response wrapper carries results and pagination metadata.

An empty query selects a discovery endpoint; a nonempty query selects a title-search endpoint. This is a useful separation because discovery and search answer different questions. Discovery asks which items match a set of catalogue constraints; search asks which names match text. The implementation appends filter parameters, but each endpoint's supported parameters still determine their effect.

Streaming-provider requests currently use the US region. The source therefore supports provider filtering, but it does not establish availability in every user's country.

### Use a compound identity for mixed catalogues
Watched and watchlist records carry both a numeric ID and a content type. Before inserting a record, Rust removes an existing record with the same pair. That prevents a movie and a TV show with the same numeric ID from being treated as one item.

The same identity rule belongs everywhere: card state, membership checks, deletion, and persistence. If one path compares only the numeric ID, an apparently minor shortcut can corrupt the user's intent across two catalogues.

### Combine in-memory state with durable snapshots
Rust holds the API key and both lists in mutex-protected application state. The configuration directory contains separate JSON files for configuration, watched items, and the watchlist. List mutations update memory and serialize a snapshot; retrieval can load persisted records back into state.

JSON makes the storage easy to inspect and back up. The tradeoff is that each mutation rewrites a list, and a direct file write is not an atomic commit. The API key is also persisted in configuration rather than an operating-system credential vault; local storage alone should not be described as encryption.

### Design the surrounding states
The frontend distinguishes loading, empty, error, and result views. Pagination appends new cards rather than replacing the whole list, while missing poster paths use a fallback immediately. Trailer selection happens in Rust, keeping another piece of API interpretation outside the rendering code.

## Result
The [MoviNight repository](https://github.com/mahostar/MoviNight) contains a complete discovery-to-tracking workflow built around a small command interface. Its most reusable idea is pairing a web UI with native persistence while keeping media identity consistent across lists.

This case study is based on source inspection, rather than a new installer or performance benchmark. Platform support and speed need separate runtime verification; the README's operating-system claims are not treated as measured compatibility here.

## What I would improve
I would reuse a configured HTTP client with timeouts and explicit status handling, make provider region selectable, and add cancellation or request-version guards so an older search cannot overwrite newer results. Persistence should write a temporary file and replace the destination atomically, while API keys should use platform credential storage.

The most useful tests would exercise movie/TV ID collisions, malformed saved JSON, interrupted writes, and pagination after a filter change. These target the boundaries that can damage a watchlist, rather than merely checking that a card renders.

Source references: [Rust commands and persistence](https://github.com/mahostar/MoviNight/blob/main/src-tauri/src/lib.rs), [shipped JavaScript frontend](https://github.com/mahostar/MoviNight/blob/main/dist/main.js).

data.title: NiotoShield
data.summary: CUDA-ready vehicle vision security: anti-spoofing, embeddings, and controlled access.

projects.body:
## Problem

NiotoShield asks a difficult edge-AI question: how can a vehicle-security device decide quickly enough to be useful, without treating every detected face as trustworthy? Face recognition alone is not sufficient. A printed portrait or replayed screen can pass a recognizer unless liveness is checked first.

The system therefore needs two distinct gates: an anti-spoofing decision before identity matching, then a local authorization decision after a match. It also needs a safe way to refresh the enrolled identities without shipping a new firmware image every time a profile changes.

## What I built

I built NiotoShield as a graduation project that joins a camera, Raspberry Pi software, custom electronics, cloud-backed enrollment, and a vehicle-access output. The device is provisioned with a product key, synchronizes its owner profile from Supabase, converts the approved images into local face embeddings, and keeps the recognition path local at scan time.

The public [NiotoShield firmware repository](https://github.com/mahostar/NiotoShield-Firmware) documents the provisioning and recognition side: environment-based credentials, product-key lookup, image download, update tracking, embedding generation, and local matching. It deliberately avoids keeping the downloaded enrollment photos after embeddings are generated.

The liveness side became [EasyShield](/projects/easyshield), a separate open-source anti-spoofing project. That separation matters: NiotoShield owns the access-control flow, while EasyShield owns the data preparation, model training, evaluation, and live Real/Fake inference workflow.

## How it works
<ProjectFigure src="/images/projects/nioto-enrollment-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Cloud enrollment update and local identity embedding cache" caption="Figure 1. Product-key profile lookup and update checks control photo downloads; the device generates local embeddings and removes temporary photos afterward. Icons and metadata fields are schematic." />


### A two-gate vision path

The runtime in `face_security.py` captures a short set of face images. EasyShield evaluates the frames for spoofing before the recognizer compares identity embeddings. Real predictions must outnumber fake predictions; a failed liveness decision ends the flow. A verified face is compared with the locally stored enrollment vectors, and a match at or above the configured similarity threshold authorizes the access output.

The design is intentionally ordered this way. Running identity matching on an unverified face would make the recognizer the first security boundary, which is the wrong place to detect a printed or replayed attack. Anti-spoofing reduces that risk before the access relay is involved.

### Enrollment and synchronization

The firmware uses the device product key to retrieve the associated user profile. It compares the profile's `updated_at` value with its last successful synchronization, so it only rebuilds the local image and embedding data when the enrollment changes. This keeps the recognition path independent from round-trip cloud latency while allowing a profile to be updated remotely.

InsightFace generates the face embeddings, which are stored with metadata for later comparison. The runtime `face_security.py` uses `FACE_MATCH_THRESHOLD = 0.6`, while the README describes `0.5` and an older system diagram shows 70%. The new figure follows the executable runtime. A deployment should unify these representations and validate its chosen threshold against false-accept and false-reject rates.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/projects/nioto-gates-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Separate liveness and identity security gates before access authorization" caption="Figure 2. Presentation-attack rejection precedes local identity matching. The runtime uses a 0.6 identity threshold; the car-access illustration represents an authorization output, not a deployed barrier or a measured recognition result." />

### CUDA is part of the deployment contract

The acceleration story is about the whole inference stack, not a CUDA label on a project. EasyShield documents a CUDA 11.8 and cuDNN 8.9.6 setup with a CUDA-enabled PyTorch build (`cu118`) for its YOLOv12-nano anti-spoofing model. Its published 8,000-image evaluation reports a 75.47 ms average inference time, while the hardware sequence diagram frames a sub-80 ms analysis target. Those figures describe the model evaluation and design target; they are not a guarantee of end-to-end latency on every device or camera.

For an NVIDIA edge target such as Jetson, the deployment path is JetPack, CUDA, cuDNN, and TensorRT. CUDA accelerates the neural-network work; camera capture, decoding, data movement, thresholding, cloud synchronization, and relay actuation still have their own cost. Treating these as separate stages is how I reason about whether a vision pipeline can feel real-time rather than only reporting a fast model benchmark.

The reviewed Raspberry Pi runtime explicitly loads the liveness model on CPU. The CUDA/cuDNN environment describes model training and a possible NVIDIA target, rather than acceleration already active in this Pi code. A committed TensorRT engine or INT8 calibration pipeline was not established by the reviewed source.

## Result

NiotoShield demonstrates a complete security chain: provisioned profile sync, local embedding generation, anti-spoofing before matching, a thresholded identity decision, and a physical authorization step. The result is a more credible edge-security architecture than a standalone face-recognition demo because the model, identity store, update mechanism, and output action all have a defined place.

EasyShield supports the model side with its own [open-source repository](https://github.com/mahostar/EasyShield_v2.5): YOLOv12-nano training tools, MTCNN-assisted face preparation, live testing, and CUDA-aware environment guidance. Together, the two repositories show the link between model work and a hardware system that can use it.

## What I would improve

The next technical milestone is a measured edge deployment. I would profile camera-to-decision latency stage by stage on the target hardware, publish the camera resolution and batch policy, and separate anti-spoofing latency from face-embedding and similarity latency. On Jetson, I would export and validate a TensorRT engine, test FP16 first, then evaluate INT8 only with a representative calibration set and accuracy checks.

I would also unify the matching threshold across the design diagram and firmware, test replay attacks and poor lighting, rotate product credentials, make synchronization recover safely after interruption, and document the relay's fail-safe behavior. Those details turn a promising vision pipeline into an auditable access-control system.

data.title: Plantini
data.summary: Hydroponic towers connecting custom sensing, ESP32 firmware, and in-house fabrication.
data.paperTitle: A modular hydroponic tower with buffered root-zone water and connected sensing

projects.body:
## Abstract
Plantini combines a modular, fabricated hydroponic tower with local root-zone water retention, proprietary conductivity-based sensing, and a connected control interface. The mechanical design separates the shared reservoir from small water pockets at individual plant sites. These pockets buffer the interval between refill pulses, allowing the main pump to operate intermittently while plants retain access to water. The author describes a one-minute-per-hour refill schedule and approximately 10–24 hours of local reserve depending on plant uptake. This paper develops the corresponding water-balance and pump-duty models, relates the functional diagrams to the supplied CAD/video and assembled tower, and describes the measurement-to-interface responsibilities without publishing the sensor's construction or calibration recipe.

**Keywords:** hydroponic tower; local water reserve; intermittent pumping; modular CAD; conductivity sensing; connected control.

<ProjectAlbum />

## System specification
