### 2.1 Mechanical hierarchy
The prototype record includes the tower module CAD, base CAD views, printed growing cups, an assembled tower with lighting, and the planted tower. The assembled system uses vertically stacked modules with angled plant sites, a supporting base, and external curved lighting arms. Removable growing cups provide access to individual plants while the tower body organizes the shared physical structure.

The CAD video exposes the angled growing-cup/socket geometry from multiple orientations. It informs the new cutaway drawings, while the water-retention function comes from the author's explanation of the design. A colored CAD selection is not a water simulation. The figures are functional illustrations, with fabrication dimensions and sensor internals omitted.

### 2.2 Three interacting physical domains
The nutrient reservoir supplies the hydraulic loop; a local water pocket supports the root zone between refill events; external lighting serves the canopy. These have different time scales and power requirements. The pumping schedule therefore should not be read as a lighting schedule or a whole-device energy budget.

| Domain | Physical responsibility | Available evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tower / cups / base | Support, plant-site access, modular assembly | CAD, printing and prototype photographs |
| Shared water loop | Refill and recirculation | Assembled system and author's operating description |
| Root-zone pocket | Retain a small local water reserve | CAD-informed functional interpretation |
| Sensing | Conductivity-related response and temperature context | Private research and supplied firmware |
| Operator interface | Profiles, readings, calibration and equipment state | Existing app screenshots |

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/plantini/research/tower-assembly-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Modular hydroponic tower assembly" caption="Figure 1. CAD/photo-informed assembly hierarchy and functional interfaces. The exploded section is schematic, without fabrication dimensions." />

## Method
### 3.1 A local reserve changes the hydraulic requirement
Continuous pumping ties root access to continuous circulation. A retained pocket separates those requirements: a refill pulse replenishes water locally, then plant uptake and losses gradually reduce the reserve while the pump is off. Excess water returns through the shared circulation path; the pocket preserves a smaller volume at the plant site.

Let $V_p$ denote usable retained water, $q_{\mathrm{in}}$ refill flow, $q_u$ uptake, and $q_\ell$ combined evaporation and other losses. A lumped balance is

$$
\frac{\mathrm dV_p}{\mathrm dt}
=q_{\mathrm{in}}-q_u-q_\ell.
\tag{1}
$$

Between refill events, $q_{\mathrm{in}}=0$. Under an approximately constant demand, the reserve duration is

$$
\tau_{\mathrm{reserve}}\approx
\frac{V_{p,\mathrm{usable}}}{q_u+q_\ell}.
\tag{2}
$$

The author describes roughly 10–24 hours depending on plant absorption. This operating description is conditional: reserve volume, root access, plant size, environment, and losses affect duration. It is not a universal irrigation guarantee or a measured endurance curve. Root aeration and refill distribution remain relevant alongside water availability.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/plantini/research/root-pocket-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Root-zone water pocket cutaway" caption="Figure 2. CAD-informed growing-cup section showing refill, retained water and root uptake. The 10–24 h reserve is the author’s operating description." />

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/plantini/research/water-circuit-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Tower recirculation and local buffering" caption="Figure 3. Functional reservoir–tower recirculation with upward supply, gravity return and local buffering at plant sites. Internal routing is schematic." />

### 3.2 Intermittent pumping and the energy model
For one minute of pump operation in each hour, the duty ratio $D$ and daily pump runtime are

$$
\begin{aligned}
D&=\frac{1\ \mathrm{min}}{60\ \mathrm{min}}=\frac1{60}\approx1.67\%,\\
t_{\mathrm{on,day}}&=24\ \mathrm{min}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
$$

At unchanged on-state pump power $P_{\mathrm{on}}$, an idealized daily energy model gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_{\mathrm{pump}}&\approx P_{\mathrm{on}}D\,(24\ \mathrm h),\\
\frac{E_{\mathrm{pulse}}}{E_{\mathrm{continuous}}}&\approx\frac1{60}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
$$

The analytical reduction applies to pump runtime and ideal pump energy. It excludes controller standby, lighting, startup losses, pump operating-point changes, and refill efficacy. No electrical power measurements are inferred from the CAD or screenshots.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/plantini/research/pump-duty-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Intermittent pump duty-cycle analysis" caption="Figure 4. Analytical one-minute-per-hour schedule: 1.67% duty and 24 min of daily pump runtime. The ideal energy ratio applies only to the pump." />

### 3.3 Conductivity sensing as a calibrated proxy
The in-house sensing work uses an alternating measurement approach to obtain a conductivity-related response while avoiding a persistent DC bias. The research code includes repeated-cycle validation, temperature handling, calibration persistence, and separate invalid/saturated outcomes. Public explanation stops at these operating responsibilities; the excitation circuit, electrode geometry, timings, parts values, and fitted calibration parameters remain private.

Conductivity reflects the water's combined ionic composition. A general physical representation is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\kappa&=K_{\mathrm{cell}}G,\\
\kappa_{25}&\approx\frac{\kappa_T}{1+\alpha(T-25)},\\
C_{\mathrm{TDS}}&\approx f_{\mathrm{solution}}\kappa_{25}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
$$

Here $G$ is conductance, $K_{\mathrm{cell}}$ a calibrated cell factor, $\alpha$ a temperature coefficient, and $f_{\mathrm{solution}}$ a composition-dependent conversion factor. These symbolic public relationships are not the proprietary production calibration equation. A TDS estimate cannot identify individual nutrient ions; temperature and composition matter to its interpretation. [USGS water-quality measurement background](https://water.usgs.gov/nwc/NWC/water_quality/tables/quality.abs.html).

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/plantini/research/conductivity-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Conductivity sensing and TDS interpretation" caption="Figure 5. Public conductivity and temperature-compensation principles; solution-dependent conversion and measurement context. Private sensor construction remains omitted." />

## Implementation
### 4.1 Measurement, controller, and cloud responsibilities
The supplied Plantini firmware examples divide sensor processing from ESP32 control. Their handoff carries a reading together with status, quality, validity, and health information. The example controller requests readings and diagnostics over a serial interface, handles response timeouts, and distinguishes a valid measurement from an error response.

The author describes Firebase as the app/device synchronization layer. The architecture figure therefore separates sensor processing, controller state, shared cloud state, and the mobile interface. The supplied material establishes the sensing handoff and visible interface responsibilities; it does not establish the Flutter application's internal subscriptions or production database schema.

### 4.2 Configuration and observable state
The existing dashboard presents TDS, temperature, pH, pump state, and lighting state. The configuration screen provides a crop profile, a sensor-calibration action, and Always / Normal / Eco pump-mode choices. The captured numbers are interface states, not universal nutrient targets or plant-growth trial results.

The three mode labels demonstrate a control surface. Their exact production timing rules are not inferred from the labels. The one-minute-per-hour schedule discussed above is the author's hydraulic operating description. Likewise, a pH card does not by itself document a pH sensor implementation in the supplied TDS firmware.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/plantini/research/growth-lighting-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Tower plant sites and external lighting" caption="Figure 6. Source-informed tower, removable plant sites and external curved lighting. Water delivery and canopy lighting are separate coupled requirements." />

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/plantini/research/operator-loop-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Plantini sensing and operator loop" caption="Figure 7. Firmware-example sensor handoff, author-described Firebase synchronization and controls visible in the existing app screens." />

## Evidence
### 5.1 Mechanical and interface record
The gallery retains original tower and base CAD views, the CAD rotation video, printed cups, assembly photographs, the planted tower, PCB/product media, and app screens. The new figures make the relationships between these artifacts explicit: assembly hierarchy, root-pocket section, recirculation, duty cycle, canopy lighting, measurement interpretation, and the operator loop.

CAD and photographs document geometry and assembly. The CAD-informed cutaway depicts an operating mechanism; it is not finite-element or fluid-dynamics validation. The author-provided refill and reserve durations are distinguished from the analytical duty calculation. Sensor research describes implementation work and validation procedures, without introducing an unsupported accuracy specification.

### 5.2 In-house sensing research
The author reports four months of sensing research aimed at making the technology understandable and manufacturable in-house. The inspected research and supplied firmware show attention to calibration, measurement status, temperature assumptions, and sensor/controller separation. They are used here to explain engineering decisions without distributing the build details.

## Discussion
Local buffering is the central mechanical idea: the device can replenish water periodically while maintaining a reserve at each root site. Its benefit depends on distribution across plant sites, usable pocket volume, plant demand, and losses. A useful validation record would pair refill uniformity, reserve depletion, root condition, and measured electrical energy over the same operating interval.

Connected sensing adds a second engineering requirement: the operator must understand whether a number is current, valid, calibrated, and associated with measured or assumed temperature. Bulk TDS trends support solution management, while nutrient-specific composition and crop outcomes require additional evidence. The paper presents the working design and source responsibilities without converting interface values or conceptual diagrams into performance claims.

## References
- Project CAD/media record: tower module, base front/side, growing-cup rotation video, assembled tower/light and planted tower, retained in the gallery below.
- Owner-supplied Plantini firmware: `esp32-usage-example.ino`, the paired TDS production examples, and sensor health/validity interfaces; inspected read-only.
- Private in-house research: measurement library, technical report and validation protocol in the supplied TDS research folder; construction and fitted parameters withheld from the public page.
- [USGS water-quality measurement principles](https://water.usgs.gov/nwc/NWC/water_quality/tables/quality.abs.html).

data.title: Remote PC Power Control
data.summary: An Ethernet-connected relay and dual heartbeats for remote PC power control and visibility.

projects.body:
## Problem
Remote desktop software cannot help when the computer is powered down. Solving that requires a control path that stays available independently of the PC, plus feedback about whether the controller and operating system are reachable.

A motherboard power button is a momentary switch, rather than an explicit “turn on” command. The same press can start a powered-down machine or request shutdown from a running one, depending on its state and operating-system configuration.

## What I built
The project combines a WT32-ETH01 Ethernet-connected ESP32 board, a relay across the motherboard's power-button contacts, Firebase Realtime Database, and a Node.js heartbeat process on the PC. A Flutter control application is described in the architecture; the reviewed folder contains firmware, the PC service, and design documents.

The controller has its own power supply and network connection, so it can receive a request while the PC's operating system is unavailable. This private project exposes no repository link or credentials through the portfolio.

## How it works
<ProjectFigure src="/images/projects/remote-control-styled.webp" width={1768} height={889} alt="Independent PC power-button control and dual heartbeat paths" caption="Figure 1. An app command reaches the independently powered Ethernet controller, whose relay briefly bridges the motherboard button contacts. Controller and OS-service heartbeats both write to the database. Hardware and interface drawings are functional schematics." />

### Translate a request into a physical action
The control interface sets a cloud command flag. In the continuously connected firmware, a database stream delivers updates to the controller. The callback records a request; the main loop handles a one-second relay pulse and returns the relay to its inactive state.

Keeping pulse timing outside the callback avoids holding the physical action inside the network event handler. The design also separates the persistent stream from ordinary command-reset and heartbeat writes.

A successful pulse says the controller acted. It does not establish that the PC booted successfully or completed shutdown.

### Clear stale commands before accepting new ones
The connected firmware blocks relay activation while a command reset remains unconfirmed. On startup, it clears an old pending command before allowing ordinary operation. After a pulse, it resets the flag and retries failed writes.

This matters during reboot and network recovery. A flag left true must not be interpreted as a new click every time a connection returns. The guard is useful, but a boolean still lacks a unique request identity and expiration time.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/projects/remote-pulse-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Relay request, timed pulse and confirmed command-reset state machine" caption="Figure 2. The connected production firmware gates new requests until reset is confirmed, times a one-second pulse in the main loop, and retries command-reset writes every second. Relay ON/OFF here describes the contact pulse, not confirmed PC power state." />

### Observe two independent systems
The controller publishes its own heartbeat, while the PC service updates a separate timestamp every five seconds. The service uses the database's server timestamp, avoiding dependence on the PC's local clock for the stored value. It sends immediately at startup and continues periodically.

When the service stops, it leaves the last timestamp intact. The interface can interpret its age to decide whether contact is fresh. Separate heartbeats distinguish “the controller is reachable” from “the PC service is reporting.”

A stale PC heartbeat can mean shutdown, a crash, a stopped service, or a network outage. The honest state is “not reporting,” rather than a definitive claim about electrical power. This uncertainty matters when another press could affect an already-running machine.

### Explore latency against active time
The folder includes a deep-sleep firmware variant. It wakes periodically to check for a request, performs a pulse when needed, publishes periodic heartbeats, and returns to sleep. The sleep interval is ten seconds, with ordinary heartbeats every third wake cycle.

This reduces active time but adds polling delay and repeated connection setup. It also handles pending commands differently from the connected firmware. These are alternative strategies, rather than interchangeable guarantees; selecting one requires tests of response time, reconnect behavior, and command replay under failure.

## Result
The implementation provides an independent hardware action path and separate controller/PC visibility. It addresses a part of remote access that desktop software cannot supply: requesting a physical button action before an operating system is available.

The practical lesson is to separate requested intent, controller execution, and observed PC availability. They are related signals, but none safely substitutes for the others. This article describes the source and architecture rather than claiming a new hardware endurance or power-consumption test.

## What I would improve
I would replace the boolean flag with expiring requests carrying unique IDs, then record acknowledgements for receipt and execution. The interface should distinguish fresh contact, stale contact, and unknown state, with a deliberate action when the PC state is uncertain.

Recovery tests should cover a connection lost immediately after a pulse, failed acknowledgement, reboot with a pending request, and a heartbeat service that stops while the PC remains running. For the sleep variant, measuring wake-to-action latency and actual energy use would establish whether the tradeoff is worthwhile.

data.title: Shrinkify
data.summary: A Python media optimizer coordinating image engines and hardware-aware FFmpeg encoding.

projects.body:
## Problem
A single quality slider cannot express every compression decision. JPEG, PNG, WebP, and video have different encoders, different failure modes, and different relationships between quality and file size. A useful desktop tool must coordinate those differences without making the user build command lines for every file.

Shrinkify wraps that coordination in a Python and Tkinter application for Windows. The interesting work is the decision pipeline behind the interface: inspect the source, choose a format-specific strategy, run the encoder, and check whether the output actually helps.

## What I built
The main application coordinates Pillow, MozJPEG, pngquant, oxipng, FFmpeg, and ffprobe. It provides single-image and folder workflows, video batch processing, theme switching, saved configuration, and progress and diagnostic views.

External executables are resolved from an `engine` directory and checked at startup. Those binaries are distributed separately from the source. This keeps the Python repository smaller, while making dependency discovery and packaging part of the product experience.

## How it works
### Choose a strategy for each format
JPEG optimization prefers MozJPEG when available and falls back to Pillow. PNG optimization can try lossy palette quantization through pngquant, then lossless optimization through oxipng, then a Pillow fallback. WebP uses Pillow's encoder with a configured quality and method.

These paths have different semantics. Palette quantization can change pixels; lossless PNG optimization changes the representation without intentionally changing the image. Presenting both as one generic quality promise would hide the decision the user is making.

The intelligent image path inspects characteristics such as dimensions and image complexity, then chooses settings for the selected profile. After encoding, it compares output size with the original. If the result is no smaller, it copies the original instead. This size guard belongs to that optimization path; it is not a universal guarantee for every action in the application.

### Keep expensive work off the UI thread
Image and video batches run on background threads. Logs, progress updates, completion messages, and button state changes are scheduled back through Tkinter's `root.after` mechanism. That lets a long-running encoder finish without forcing the interface's event loop to do the encoding itself.

The distinction is useful: the external process performs compression, Python coordinates it, and the UI receives updates. The current subprocess calls often capture output until completion, so the diagnostic panel should not be mistaken for a continuous FFmpeg frame-progress stream.

### Probe before choosing a video command
ffprobe supplies video metadata used to select quality, frame-rate, bitrate, and audio settings. The command builder can choose NVIDIA NVENC, Intel Quick Sync, AMD AMF, or software `libx264`. When a hardware attempt fails, the worker retries with CPU encoding.

The software branch uses CRF and a preset, while hardware branches use encoder-specific quality controls. Reusing one numeric setting does not make those controls perceptually equivalent. A future tuning pass needs separate calibration for each encoder.

The reviewed command builder emits H.264, adds MP4 fast-start metadata and `yuv420p`, and conditionally encodes audio as AAC. Although the README mentions H.265, this particular implementation path does not justify advertising a working H.265 selector.

## Result
The [Shrinkify repository](https://github.com/mahostar/Shrinkify) demonstrates an orchestration approach to media optimization: established encoders do the specialist work, while Python supplies selection, fallback, batch handling, and understandable feedback.

The reusable lesson is that compression success has two dimensions: the process must complete, and the output must be worth keeping. The image size guard addresses the second dimension without claiming that lossy compression preserves identical visual quality. No compression ratio or throughput benchmark is claimed here.

## What I would improve
I would add cancellation, subprocess timeouts, and incremental FFmpeg progress parsing. Worker inputs should be captured from UI controls before launching a thread, keeping Tkinter access on its owning thread. Encoder selection and quality settings should move into separately testable modules; the current file also repeats a video-settings method, which makes maintenance harder.

A meaningful validation set would include transparent PNGs, animated images, JPEGs with metadata, portrait videos, clips without audio, and failing GPU encoders. Each check should compare readability, dimensions, retained metadata, output size, and visual differences. Smaller output alone is insufficient evidence of a successful media transformation.

Source references: [compression and worker implementation](https://github.com/mahostar/Shrinkify/blob/main/Production-Ready-ts-darkMode.py), [engine setup](https://github.com/mahostar/Shrinkify/blob/main/engine/README.md).

data.title: SmartHart
data.summary: A simulated vital-sign pipeline with seven-feature sequence classification and live charts.
data.paperTitle: Sequence classification of simulated vital signs with a live inference dashboard

projects.body:
## Abstract
SmartHart implements an end-to-end experimental pipeline for simulated multivariate vital signs: labeled data generation, seven-feature sequence construction, bidirectional recurrent classification, and online visualization. A ten-observation window is classified using the state attached to its final observation. The runtime reuses the training scaler and label map, maintains a sliding buffer, and displays predictions alongside the simulator's known labels. This paper describes the tensor contract, model architecture, training/runtime window differences, and a preprocessing-order issue relevant to evaluation. The system is a simulation-based academic prototype; the repository's reported accuracy describes synthetic scenarios rather than clinical performance.

**Keywords:** synthetic time series; sequence classification; bidirectional LSTM; feature consistency; online inference; monitoring interface.

## System specification
### 2.1 Data generation and labels
The simulator emits systolic and diastolic blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, a timestamp, and a scenario label. The default generation interval is 0.5 seconds. Scenario dynamics couple changes across signals over time; labels include normal, cardiac-arrest, hypertensive-crisis, and septic-shock simulations.

These names identify synthetic generator scenarios. They do not constitute diagnoses produced or validated on patient recordings. The dashboard's controls adjust generation interval, plot history, and anomaly probability, allowing the same inference path to be exercised under different simulated transition rates.

### 2.2 Seven-feature tensor contract
Five generated measurements are supplemented with two derived features: pulse pressure $P_P$ and a guarded heart-rate-to-systolic-pressure ratio $S_I$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_P&=P_{\mathrm{sys}}-P_{\mathrm{dia}},\\
S_I&=\frac{H_R}{P_{\mathrm{sys}}+10^{-6}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{1}
$$

The feature order is fixed: systolic pressure, diastolic pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate, pulse pressure, and the ratio above. Training and runtime must use the same order and persisted scaler. Each completed model input has shape $X\in\mathbb R^{B\times10\times7}$, with batch size $B=1$ for an online prediction.

## Method
### 3.1 Chronology, scaling, and window labels
Training validates required columns, parses timestamps, removes invalid rows, sorts observations chronologically, and derives the two additional features. `StandardScaler` transforms each feature using a saved mean and scale:

$$
\widetilde{x}_{t,j}=\frac{x_{t,j}-\mu_j}{\sigma_j}.
\tag{2}
$$

The default sequence length is ten and the training overlap parameter is zero, yielding stride ten. A sequence receives the label from its final row. An 80/20 chronological training/test split is made without shuffling. Keras reserves 20% of the training portion for validation.

The inspected preprocessing fits the scaler before splitting the sequences. Test-period feature distributions therefore influence the scaling parameters. A strict held-out evaluation should fit preprocessing only on training observations and apply those parameters to later periods. This is an evaluation boundary in the original implementation, which remains unchanged.

### 3.2 Bidirectional recurrent classifier
The first bidirectional LSTM has 128 units per direction and returns the full sequence, giving a $10\times256$ representation per sample. A second bidirectional LSTM has 64 units per direction and returns a 128-element vector. A 64-unit ReLU dense layer precedes the class softmax; dropout of 0.2 follows each recurrent stage and the intermediate dense layer.

For logits $z_c$ and final-row class $y$, the classifier uses

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_c&=\frac{e^{z_c}}{\sum_{k=1}^{C}e^{z_k}},\\
\mathcal L&=-\log p_y.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
$$

The inspected training configuration uses Adam with learning rate $10^{-3}$, batch size 32, and a maximum of 30 epochs. Early stopping monitors validation loss with patience five and restores weights from the minimum validation loss. $C$ is determined by the encoded labels; the supplied generator defines four scenario classes.

Bidirectional processing operates inside the already observed ten-row window. It does not require observations beyond that completed window at online inference time.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/smarthart/research/sequence-classifier-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Seven-feature BiLSTM sequence contract" caption="Figure 1. Five simulated measurements become seven features and ten-row model inputs. Shapes follow the inspected recurrent architecture and saved artifact contract." />

## Implementation
### 4.1 A three-artifact inference contract
Training saves the Keras model, fitted scaler, and class-label array. Runtime loads all three: the model alone is insufficient because its inputs depend on feature scaling and its numeric outputs depend on the persisted class order.

The online process computes the same seven features, transforms them with the saved scaler, reshapes the buffer to $(1,10,7)$, and maps the softmax argmax through the saved labels. It waits for ten observations before predicting.

### 4.2 Sliding online inference and UI scheduling
Training uses non-overlapping windows by default. Runtime advances the ten-row buffer by one observation, so neighboring predictions share nine rows. This provides frequent interface updates while introducing strong temporal dependence between adjacent decisions.

A background data loop generates observations and invokes the Tkinter scheduler for interface updates. The dashboard redraws live signal charts and prediction state through the UI event loop. Adjustable history length affects the displayed trace; the classifier's input length remains ten.

The runtime compares each prediction with the simulator's current known label. Its displayed moving accuracy uses the most recent 100 prediction outcomes:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_t&=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{k=t-m+1}^{t}\mathbf{1}[\hat y_k=y_k],\\
m&=\min(100,n).
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
$$

Here $n$ is the number of available prediction outcomes. This is an online diagnostic on overlapping synthetic windows, rather than an independent test-set estimate.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/smarthart/research/streaming-dashboard-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="Sliding-window inference dashboard" caption="Figure 2. Ten-row online windows advance by one observation and share nine rows. UI state compares predictions with known synthetic labels over recent outcomes." />

## Evidence
The repository README reports overall accuracy above 98% and approximately 93% for online operation. Those values are source-reported simulation results; no training or patient-data evaluation was rerun for this page. The training script provides confusion-matrix, classification-report, and ROC analysis code, while the live interface exposes scenario labels, predictions, and recent correctness.

The existing application and project media remain available in the gallery. New source-derived figures explain the feature/model contract and online state transition without inventing signal recordings, accuracy curves, or patient measurements.

## Discussion
The project demonstrates consistency across data generation, feature engineering, artifact persistence, inference, and visualization. Its most useful implementation distinctions are final-row sequence labels, training stride ten versus runtime stride one, and the dependence of every inference on a matched scaler and label map.

Further evaluation should isolate preprocessing to the training period, separate complete simulated episodes across splits, and report transition-level errors in addition to aggregate accuracy. Class imbalance and long normal intervals can hide missed scenario transitions. Results on this generator establish behavior within its synthetic assumptions; real sensor variability, missingness, and clinical generalization remain outside the demonstrated evaluation.

## References

projects.body:
## Abstract
TPMS Studio converts parameterized implicit fields into finite, closed triangle meshes through a reproducible desktop workflow. Periodic equations describe the geometry; cell counts and domain dimensions set its spatial frequency; a scalar-field band creates material around the level surface. A negative exterior padding layer closes intersections at the sampled domain boundary before marching-cubes extraction. Vertex cleanup, normal correction, and topology inspection complete the path to preview and STL export. This paper traces that implementation, separates geometric fidelity from mesh closure, and reports a fresh source-copy check of six built-in presets. All six checked meshes were watertight under the stated test configuration.

**Keywords:** implicit geometry; TPMS; marching cubes; shell generation; boundary closure; mesh topology.

<ProjectAlbum />

## System specification
### 2.1 A geometry engine with an observable desktop interface
The reviewed implementation is the Python engine in `tpms_generator.py` and its PyQt5/PyVistaQt interface in `GUI_API.py`. The repository also contains a React/Three.js educational viewer; that viewer is a separate presentation path. The mesh-generation architecture below describes the desktop tool.

The API accepts a `TPMSConfig`, returns a `TPMSResult`, and exports its retained mesh. The GUI exposes template and custom-expression controls, requests generation through a worker thread, and presents the result as a colored surface or wireframe. API configuration supports independent dimensions and cell counts on each axis; the reviewed GUI uses one size and one cell count for all three axes.

| Configuration | Geometric or computational role |
| --- | --- |
| Formula | Gyroid, Primitive, Diamond, IWP, Neovius, or BCC; custom expressions are also supported |
| Physical dimensions $L_x,L_y,L_z$ | Coordinate scale of the sampled domain |
| Cell counts $n_x,n_y,n_z$ | Repetition density along each axis |
| Isovalue $C$ | Offset applied to the evaluated field |
| Field-band parameter $\tau$ | Width of the retained interval in scalar-field values |
| Grid resolution $r_x,r_y,r_z$ | Sampling density before surface extraction |
| Target file size | Heuristic input to automatic resolution selection |

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/tpms-generator/research/tpms-software-styled.webp" width={1659} height={948} alt="TPMS Studio desktop configuration, worker, geometry API, topology inspection and export" caption="Figure 1. The source-derived desktop workflow. Expensive generation runs in a QThread; the returned mesh and status feed preview and export." />

## Method
### 3.1 Spatial frequency makes the model reproducible
For axis $a\in\{x,y,z\}$, the engine derives angular frequency from the requested number of repetitions and physical domain length:

$$
\omega_a=\frac{2\pi n_a}{L_a},\qquad \theta_a=\omega_a x_a.
\tag{1}
$$

This binds the periodic rule to physical coordinates. Increasing cell count while holding domain length fixed produces smaller repeated cells. Increasing domain length while holding cell count fixed increases cell size. The main presets use these axis-specific frequencies.

For the Gyroid approximation, the sampled field is

$$
\begin{aligned}
F(\mathbf x)&=\sin\theta_x\cos\theta_y\\
&\quad+\sin\theta_y\cos\theta_z\\
&\quad+\sin\theta_z\cos\theta_x-C.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
$$

The trigonometric representation is an implicit approximation used to generate TPMS-like geometry. It does not constitute a numerical proof of zero mean curvature. The engine evaluates the base preset with zero offset and then subtracts the configured $C$ once. This makes the isovalue a geometric input rather than a display adjustment.

### 3.2 Material is a band around the level surface
A zero level set has no solid thickness. The generator transforms the field into a sign convention suitable for a solid shell:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S(\mathbf x)&=\frac{\tau}{2}-|F(\mathbf x)|,\\
\Omega_{\mathrm{solid}}&=\{\mathbf x:S(\mathbf x)\geq0\}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
$$

The two sides of the shell lie near $F=\pm\tau/2$. The parameter named `wall_thickness` in the source acts directly on field values. Because $F$ is not a signed-distance function, this parameter does not generally produce a constant thickness in millimetres. Where the field has a nonzero gradient and the band is sufficiently narrow, a local first-order estimate is

$$
t_{\mathrm{local}}(\mathbf x)\approx\frac{\tau}{\|\nabla F(\mathbf x)\|}.
\tag{4}
$$

This distinction explains why numerical resolution and physical feature inspection both matter. A band can be mathematically well specified while its local wall width varies through the part. A constant-distance offset would require a distance-field construction or another thickness-control method.

### 3.3 Boundary closure is an explicit construction
The sampled shell may intersect the sides of the finite box. Extracting only the interior can leave boundary loops open. The engine pads every side with one voxel of exterior value $S=-1$, then extracts the zero level. Interpolation between interior solid values and the negative exterior creates closure surfaces at those cuts.

Marching cubes converts local grid-cell crossings into vertices and triangular faces. The resulting padded-grid vertex coordinate $v_a$ is transformed into physical units by

$$
x_a=(v_a-1)\frac{L_a}{r_a-1}.
\tag{5}
$$

Subtracting one removes the padding-index offset; dividing by $r_a-1$ accounts for the inclusive grid endpoints. Closure occurs between the boundary samples and the exterior layer, so the final mesh bounds can extend slightly beyond the nominal sampling box. Exact manufactured extents should be checked on the extracted mesh.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/tpms-generator/research/tpms-geometry-styled.webp" width={1660} height={948} alt="Implicit TPMS field, solid band, exterior padding, marching cubes and closed mesh checks" caption="Figure 2. Scalar-field banding and negative exterior padding provide a closed-shell construction. Topology is checked on the resulting mesh; the band is not a signed-distance thickness." />

### 3.4 Resolution is selected before extraction
The automatic controller estimates triangle count from a requested binary-STL payload and approximates the relation between triangles and voxels. With target size $B$ in decimal megabytes, its initial cubic-grid estimate follows

$$
\begin{aligned}
\widehat T&=\frac{10^6B}{50},\\
\widehat V&=\frac{\widehat T}{0.45},\\
r_0&=\max\!\left(\lfloor\widehat V^{1/3}\rfloor,20n_{\max}\right),\\
r&=\min(300,r_0).
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}
$$

The estimate uses 50 bytes per binary-STL triangle and 0.45 triangles per voxel. Neither the realized triangle count nor the final file size is fixed by this estimate. The 300-point cap takes precedence when the cell-density floor exceeds it. Explicit resolution bypasses this automatic rule. The ordinary generation path does not automatically decimate the extracted mesh.

## Implementation
### 4.1 State and execution boundaries
`TPMSMainWindow.start_generation` gathers controls into a configuration, disables the Generate button, and starts `GenerationWorker`. Its `run` method calls `TPMSGeneratorAPI.generate`. Completion or error signals return control to the GUI, where the button is restored and a successful result becomes the current preview/export object.

Within the engine, `ResolutionController` chooses the grid, `TPMSEngine` selects the scalar-field function, and `MeshGenerator` builds the band and extracts geometry. NumPy evaluates full three-dimensional coordinate arrays. This vectorization avoids a Python loop over individual grid points, but its memory cost still grows with the number of sampled voxels. Raising every axis resolution increases the volume of work cubically.

### 4.2 What the topology report establishes
After extraction, the API merges vertices and fixes normals through Trimesh. It reports `mesh.is_watertight` and `mesh.euler_number`. Watertight edge connectivity means every mesh edge is incident to two faces. A porous solid can contain many tunnels and remain watertight: the tunnel walls are part of a closed boundary, rather than missing faces.

The Euler characteristic is

$$
\chi=V-E+T,
\tag{7}
$$

where $V$, $E$, and $T$ are mesh vertex, edge, and triangle counts. The source stores this value under a field named `genus`; this paper reports it as Euler characteristic. Converting it into genus requires additional assumptions about connectedness and orientability.

The API can return success even when watertight status is false, and export checks generation success rather than imposing a topology gate. Curvature and periodicity validator modules exist, but the reviewed main path does not execute those advanced checks. The result is an inspectable generation and topology workflow, with closure status available for each mesh.

## Evidence
### 5.1 Fresh topology check of the six main presets
For this page, the engine file was copied into an isolated temporary directory and executed using the project's existing Python environment. The original file's SHA-256 remained unchanged. No source code was modified and no training or dependency installation was required.

Each run used a $48\times48\times48$ grid, $2\times2\times2$ cells, a $20\times20\times20$ mm sampling domain, $C=0$, and field-band parameter $\tau=0.5$. All six runs returned successful meshes, reported watertight status, and independently had exactly two incident faces per unique edge.

| Preset | Triangles | Euler characteristic | Watertight |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| Gyroid | 91,884 | −102 | Yes |
| Primitive | 71,360 | −64 | Yes |
| Diamond | 113,068 | −230 | Yes |
| IWP | 91,496 | −196 | Yes |
| Neovius | 77,776 | −1,064 | Yes |
| BCC | 47,016 | −300 | Yes |

These are topology checks at one stated configuration, not mechanical, flow, or print benchmarks. The Gyroid's measured coordinate bounds were approximately $-0.0851$ to $20.0851$ mm on each axis, illustrating the small exterior extension introduced by interpolated padding caps.

### 5.2 Original visual evidence
The existing blue, green, and purple mesh screenshots remain in the project gallery. They document the desktop viewer and generated surface appearance. The two new figures explain the algorithm; their schematic geometry is not additional manufacturing evidence.

## Discussion
The central engineering decision is to construct a finite solid before extracting its boundary. Periodic evaluation, field banding, negative padding, and explicit coordinate scaling make the path reproducible; post-extraction inspection exposes whether a particular result is closed.

Closure and geometric accuracy answer different questions. Resolution determines how well the grid captures narrow features and curvature. The field gradient influences local wall width. Padding affects final bounds. A watertight flag addresses connectivity, while printing also depends on dimensions, minimum feature size, orientation, support, and material. Self-intersection and minimum-wall checks would strengthen the export contract.

Custom expressions currently use a restricted evaluation namespace. A parser with an explicit operator/function allowlist would make the contract clearer. The procedural expression helper generates symbolic candidates; the model-loading hook is a stub in this source. This paper therefore attributes the geometry to equation evaluation and numerical meshing.

## References
1. **Primary engine:** `tpms_generator.py` — `TPMSConfig`, `TPMSEngine`, `ResolutionController`, `MeshGenerator`, and `TPMSGeneratorAPI.generate/export` in the supplied TPMS Academy repository.
2. **Desktop application:** `GUI_API.py` — `GenerationWorker`, `TPMSMainWindow.start_generation`, `on_finished`, `update_view`, and `export_mesh`.
3. **Auxiliary paths:** `utils/templates.py`, `models/procedural_generator.py`, and the curvature/periodicity validation modules. Their presence is distinguished from execution in the reviewed main path.
4. **Reproduction record:** isolated source-copy topology runs on 4 October 2026; six presets and the fixed configuration listed in Section 5.1. Existing mesh screenshots are preserved in the gallery.

projects.body:
## Abstract
The motivating constraint is training-data expansion: materializing every overlapping history–forecast window from an approximately 40 GB weather archive can produce terabytes of duplicated observations. This work implements a CPU–GPU streaming method that retains the archive and constructs training examples as the model consumes them. Each example presents a historical sequence, withholds the following observations, and compares the forecast with the recorded future. A compact cumulative index addresses windows without storing them; parallel statistics, worker-local caching, and DataLoader prefetch prepare aligned tensors for GPU execution. The repository provides a supervised forecasting baseline and a separate reinforcement-learning path that samples forecasts and rewards agreement with the observed future. A reported 20-epoch experiment achieved approximately 24% under the project's relative-error-based forecast score. The central contribution is the streaming representation and training interface; the storage analysis distinguishes all possible window starts from the configured stride.

**Keywords:** training-data expansion; streaming windows; implicit indexing; CPU–GPU pipeline; reinforcement learning; ERA5.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/projects/windweave-streaming.webp" width={1600} height={900} alt="WindWeave original streaming concept artwork" caption="Concept artwork. Archived weather observations pass through CPU preparation before GPU consumption; the illustration provides a visual overview of the streaming pipeline." />

## System specification
### 2.1 Data and forecasting contract
Each location file contains a chronological observation sequence. The numeric feature vector at observation $t$ is

$$
\mathbf{x}_t = \bigl[u_{10,t},\; v_{10,t},\; p_{s,t},\; T_{2\mathrm{m},t}\bigr]^{\mathsf T} \in \mathbb{R}^{4}.
\tag{1}
$$

Here $u_{10}$ and $v_{10}$ are the two 10 m wind components, $p_s$ is surface pressure, and $T_{2\mathrm{m}}$ is 2 m temperature in degrees Celsius. The source columns are respectively `u10`, `v10`, `sp`, and `t2m_celsius`. Forecast targets contain the two wind components. Time encoding supplies four integer marks: hour, day of week, day of month, and month.

| Parameter | Symbol | Default | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Encoder length | $L$ | 45 | Observed input rows |
| Forecast length | $H$ | 27 | Future target rows |
| Decoder context | $K$ | 24 | Final observed rows retained |
| Window stride | $s$ | 9 | Start-index increment |
| Input / target channels | $d_x, d_y$ | 4 / 2 | Numeric feature dimensions |

Lengths denote observations. Interface labels use a nine-observations-per-day convention, while the dataset slices by row index; elapsed time therefore depends on the file's timestamp cadence.

### 2.2 Execution architecture
The storage layer retains location CSVs. The CPU dataset resolves sample addresses, loads the active file, normalizes a requested slice, and constructs tensors. DataLoader collates samples and prepares subsequent batches through its worker processes. The training loop transfers batches to the selected device and executes the model, loss, backward pass, and optimizer step.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/windweave/architecture-styled.webp" width={1774} height={887} alt="CPU–GPU streaming architecture" caption="Figure 1. Storage, CPU sample construction, loader prefetch, and GPU computation. The prefetch queue is supplied by PyTorch DataLoader." />

Real-time streaming here refers to training examples assembled and supplied during model execution. The input is an archive of recorded observations; this implementation does not ingest a live meteorological feed.

## Method
### 3.1 Implicit indexing of overlapping windows
Let file $j$ contain $R_j$ observation rows. With positive stride $s$, its valid window count is

$$
N_j = \begin{cases}
\left\lfloor \dfrac{R_j-L-H}{s} \right\rfloor + 1, & R_j \ge L+H,\\[4pt]
0, & R_j < L+H.
\end{cases}
\tag{2}
$$

Files with zero windows are omitted from the sample index. For the retained files, define cumulative counts $C_j$ with $C_{-1}=0$. A zero-based global sample index $i$ identifies a file, a local window number $\ell$, and its starting row $a$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
C_j &= \sum_{k=0}^{j} N_k,\\
j(i) &= \min\{j : C_j > i\},\\
\ell(i) &= i-C_{j(i)-1},\\
a(i) &= s\,\ell(i).
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
$$

`bisect_right` implements the file lookup. The selected row interval is $[a,a+L+H)$; the first $L$ rows form the history, and the final $H$ rows form the forecast target. For $F$ eligible files, sample-address metadata occupies $O(F)$ space and file lookup takes $O(\log F)$ time. File reading, feature engineering, and tensor construction are additional costs. Initialization still scans source files to count rows.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/windweave/index-styled.webp" width={1848} height={851} alt="Cumulative-offset sample lookup" caption="Figure 2. Worked example with 99-row and 117-row files: counts [4,6], cumulative offsets [4,10], and global index 6 resolving to the second file at row 18." />

A materialized collection copies overlapping observations into separate arrays. This representation stores an address and a slicing rule instead. Window lengths and stride can consequently change without exporting a new collection of window files.

### 3.2 Storage amplification and motivation
For a long file, materializing windows duplicates each interior observation approximately $(L+H)/s$ times. If archive rows and exported window rows use comparable encodings, the approximate storage ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{B_{\mathrm{windows}}}{B_{\mathrm{archive}}}
&\approx \frac{L+H}{s},\\
L+H&=45+27=72.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
$$

Enumerating every possible start ($s=1$) gives roughly 72-fold duplication: a 40 GB archive corresponds to approximately 2.88 TB of materialized history–target rows under this model. At the configured stride $s=9$, the same estimate is eight-fold, or about 320 GB. Decoder context and temporal marks add further payload if exported separately. CSV and tensor encodings differ, so these are storage estimates rather than measurements of an exported dataset.

The approximately 40 GB archive is the original design motivation supplied by the project author. Streaming retains observations once and computes a requested window through indexing and slicing. It avoids an archive-sized collection of duplicate training examples while allowing window parameters to change independently of source storage.

### 3.3 Parallel normalization by sufficient statistics
For each numeric feature, a statistics worker returns a file summary $(n,\mu,M_2)$: count, mean, and sum of squared deviations. Two summaries $A$ and $B$ are merged by

$$
\begin{aligned}
\delta &= \mu_B-\mu_A,\\
n &= n_A+n_B,\\
\mu &= \mu_A+\delta\frac{n_B}{n},\\
M_2 &= M_{2,A}+M_{2,B}+\delta^2\frac{n_A n_B}{n}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
$$

The correction term retains variation between file means. Averaging per-file standard deviations would omit this contribution. The population scale and normalization transform are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sigma &= \sqrt{M_2/n},\\
\sigma^{\ast} &= \begin{cases}1,&\sigma=0,\\\sigma,&\sigma>0,\end{cases}\\
\widetilde{x}_{t,c} &= \frac{x_{t,c}-\mu_c}{\sigma_c^{\ast}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}
$$

The source also uses unit scales when the aggregate count is at most one. The multiprocessing pool computes summaries in parallel, and the parent collects and merges them. Each worker reads a full file into a DataFrame; compact summaries reduce the retained aggregate state, but do not make individual file reads constant-memory.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/windweave/normalization-styled.webp" width={1850} height={850} alt="Parallel normalization reduction" caption="Figure 3. Independent file summaries are reduced to feature-wise means and population scales. Panel b uses an exact four-value example to illustrate the between-file correction." />

### 3.4 Aligned encoder, decoder, and target construction
For the normalized sample beginning at row $a$, the encoder and target are

$$
\begin{aligned}
X_{\mathrm{enc}} &= \widetilde{X}[a:a+L,:],\\
Y &= \widetilde{X}[a+L:a+L+H,\{u_{10},v_{10}\}].
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
$$

The decoder input concatenates the last $K$ observed rows with $H$ zero rows:

$$
X_{\mathrm{dec}} = \begin{bmatrix}
\widetilde{X}[a+L-K:a+L,:]\\
\mathbf{0}_{H\times 4}
\end{bmatrix}.
\tag{8}
$$

Temporal marks span the same encoder and decoder intervals. Future timestamps are available as conditioning information; future observed feature values remain outside the decoder input. `__getitem__` returns the following five tensors.

| Tensor | Per-sample shape | Data type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Encoder values | $L\times4$ | Float32 |
| Encoder time marks | $L\times4$ | Int64 |
| Decoder values | $(K+H)\times4$ | Float32 |
| Decoder time marks | $(K+H)\times4$ | Int64 |
| Wind targets | $H\times2$ | Float32 |

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/windweave/tensors-styled.webp" width={1721} height={914} alt="Encoder–decoder tensor alignment" caption="Figure 4. Default shapes [45,4], [45,4], [51,4], [51,4], and [27,2]. Collation adds a leading batch dimension. Matrix cells are schematic; labels specify the actual dimensions." />

## Implementation
### 4.1 Worker-local caching and access locality
Each dataset instance retains one active DataFrame, identified by its file path. Requests to the same file reuse the DataFrame. A request to a different file replaces it. Nearby windows can therefore share parsing and feature-engineering work; globally shuffled requests may repeatedly evict the active file. With multiprocessing, caches belong to individual worker dataset instances.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/windweave/locality-styled.webp" width={1808} height={870} alt="File-cache locality and prefetch tradeoff" caption="Figure 5. Local and interleaved requests produce different cache behavior. Panel c plots the analytical queued tensor payload from equation (9) for batch size 32; it excludes DataFrames and is not a memory benchmark." />

### 4.2 CPU preparation and GPU consumption
The GUI training path enables pinned host memory. Positive worker counts additionally enable persistent workers and a configurable prefetch factor. Training uses shuffled sampling, while validation uses sequential sampling. An example configuration sets eight workers and prefetch factor two.

For $W$ workers, prefetch factor $P$, and batch size $B$, the approximate queued-batch envelope and raw tensor payload per sample are

$$
\begin{aligned}
Q_{\mathrm{batches}} &\approx WP,\\
S_{\mathrm{sample}} &= 48(L+K+H)+8H\;\text{bytes},\\
M_{\mathrm{queued}} &\approx WPB\,S_{\mathrm{sample}}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
$$

The payload expression counts four Float32 values and four Int64 marks in both encoder and decoder, plus two Float32 target values per forecast row. Under the default lengths it is 4,824 bytes per sample. This estimate excludes DataFrames, process overhead, tensor metadata, currently consumed batches, pinned copies, and model memory; it is an analytical payload estimate rather than measured resident memory.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/windweave/sequence-styled.webp" width={1691} height={930} alt="Batch-production sequence" caption="Figure 6. The training loop requests a batch; CPU workers resolve indices, reuse or read a CSV, construct tensors, and return them for collation. The lower timeline shows ordering; segment widths are not measured durations." />

The loop transfers all five tensors with ordinary `.to(device)` calls. It then executes Informer or DLinear, evaluates mean squared error on the normalized wind targets, backpropagates, and updates parameters with Adam. Pinned memory supports host-to-device transfer, while this implementation does not explicitly schedule nonblocking copies or custom CUDA streams. The source establishes CPU preparation ahead of demand; copy/compute overlap and GPU utilization need runtime measurement.

### 4.3 Forecast–reward learning loop
The learning task is to provide several days of observations, predict the following period, and use the recorded future as feedback. Under the interface's nine-observations-per-day convention, 45 history rows and 27 target rows correspond to five observed days and three forecast days. Comparing a prediction with a target is shared by both training modes: the supervised path differentiates MSE, while `rl_train.py` and `rl_train_gui.py` implement a stochastic policy and a REINFORCE-style update [5].

The RL policy extends Informer with a two-component mean head and learned log standard deviations. Its sampled wind forecast acts as the action; the streamed window and temporal marks provide conditioning information:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S&=(X_{\mathrm{enc}},T_{\mathrm{enc}},X_{\mathrm{dec}},T_{\mathrm{dec}}),\\
\widehat{\mathbf y}_t&\sim\pi_\theta(\,\cdot\mid S,t),\\
\pi_\theta&=\mathcal N(\boldsymbol\mu_\theta,\operatorname{diag}(\boldsymbol\sigma_\theta^2)).
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
$$

After sampling a forecast sequence, the reward function compares it with the observed target. It combines negative component-wise mean absolute error, a temporal-alignment penalty, high-wind event agreement, and a penalty for mismatched wind-speed variability:

$$
\begin{aligned}
R&=-w_a\operatorname{MAE}(\widehat Y,Y)\\
&\quad-w_d\frac{D_{\mathrm{DTW}}(\widehat V,V)}{H}\\
&\quad+w_h\,r_{\mathrm{event}}\\
&\quad-w_v\left|\operatorname{std}(\widehat V)-\operatorname{std}(V)\right|,\\
V_t&=\sqrt{u_{10,t}^2+v_{10,t}^2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
$$

The event term is $+1$ when both sequences exceed the threshold, $-1$ when only one does, and zero when neither does. Default reward weights are one. The optional DTW calculation falls back to zero on failure. The training function receives normalized targets, so the magnitude and threshold operate in transformed coordinates unless predictions and targets are explicitly denormalized.

The intended policy-gradient objective increases the probability of forecasts receiving larger rewards, using normalized episode rewards $\widetilde R$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
J(\theta)&=\mathbb E_{\pi_\theta}[R],\\
\nabla_\theta J&=\mathbb E_{\pi_\theta}[\widetilde R\,G_\theta],\\
G_\theta&=\sum_{t=1}^{H}\nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(\widehat{\mathbf y}_t\mid S,t).
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
$$

This is an offline, reward-based forecasting formulation: historical future observations supply feedback rather than a live environment transition. The streaming method supplies the same aligned samples to either optimization route.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/windweave/feedback-styled.webp" width={1870} height={841} alt="Forecast–reward learning loop" caption="Figure 7. Historical context and withheld future feed two learning routes. The RL route samples a forecast, compares it with observations, and uses a composite reward for the intended policy update." />

### 4.4 Experiment interfaces
The training interface exposes sequence lengths, stride, batch size, worker count, prefetch depth, model selection, learning rate, and device. The prediction interface places history beside predicted and observed wind components, with controls for browsing windows and evaluating a set of windows.

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/windweave/training-preview.webp" width={1392} height={647} alt="Training configuration interface" caption="Figure 8. Source-informed interface reconstruction. Settings mirror the saved configuration; the event log is illustrative rather than a recorded execution." />

<ProjectFigure src="/images/evidence/projects/windweave/prediction-preview.webp" width={1392} height={970} alt="Forecast inspection interface" caption="Figure 9. Reconstructed input and forecast tables with synthetic display data. No forecasting model was executed to produce this preview." />

## Evidence
The implementation evidence consists of the dataset's indexing, summary reduction, active-file cache, and five-tensor return contract, together with the loader, device-transfer configuration, and separate reward-based training source [1–2,5]. Figures 1–7 explain those operations. Figures 8–9 document the interface structure using a lightweight reconstruction [3–4]. The cover is concept artwork.

### 5.1 Reported 20-epoch evaluation
The reported experiment achieved an approximately **24% forecast score after 20 epochs** [6]. This result describes performance at that training budget. It is an author-supplied evaluation result; the accompanying source inspection establishes the streaming and scoring algorithms rather than independently reproducing the experiment.

The prediction interface calls its metric an accuracy percentage. For a nonzero actual component $y$, it clips a relative-error score to the interval $[0,100]$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
A(\widehat y,y)&=100\max(0,1-r),\\
r&=\frac{|\widehat y-y|}{|y|},\quad y\ne0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
$$

When $y=0$, the score is 100 only if the prediction is also zero, and otherwise zero. Evaluation averages scores over forecast rows, the two wind components, and windows [4]. This percentage is a regression agreement score, with strong sensitivity near zero wind components. It should not be interpreted as classification accuracy or as the fraction of forecasts that are correct. The exact metric used for the reported experiment has not been independently reproduced.

| Evidence item | Result | Provenance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Training duration | 20 epochs | Author-supplied experiment report |
| Forecast score | Approximately 24% | Author-supplied experiment report |
| Streaming representation | Windows constructed during consumption | Dataset source inspection |
| Storage amplification | About 72× at stride 1; 8× at stride 9 | Analytical estimate, equation (4) |

### 5.2 Analytical and measured claims

## Discussion
### 6.1 Evaluation boundaries
The inspected dataset computes normalization before the training/validation partition is chosen. A rigorous forecasting evaluation should fit statistics exclusively on training observations and persist them for validation and inference. A split over global sample indices also requires careful interpretation: file ordering and overlapping windows can differ from a common chronological cutoff across locations. Timestamp-aware partitioning should prevent target periods from crossing evaluation boundaries.

### 6.2 Throughput and memory measurements
A reproducible RL evaluation additionally needs to validate forecast-position selection, sample-to-reward alignment, and policy-loss aggregation in the update loop. The reward-based route is documented from source separately from the saved supervised configuration; the available checkpoint files alone do not establish measured RL performance.

A reproducible pipeline experiment should record CSV reads, cache-hit rate, batch-wait latency, host memory, transfer time, and model-step time. Worker count and prefetch factor can then be varied against both throughput and memory. A file-aware block sampler could preserve local reuse while shuffling blocks; a bounded multi-file cache or columnar storage could reduce repeated parsing. These remain proposed extensions.

Input validation should establish monotonic timestamps, cadence, required columns, missing-value handling, and duplicate-row policy before window counts are computed. Checkpoints should include normalization parameters, feature order, sequence settings, partition metadata, and model configuration. These additions would make the existing streaming contract reproducible across training and prediction.

The system's principal engineering result is a separation between observation storage, sample addressing, CPU tensor construction, and GPU model execution. Its suitability for another sequence domain depends on the same alignment, locality, and evaluation constraints.
